Spring wheat requires cool temperatures (15-22°C) to produce an economically viable yield, thus in Zimbabwe it is mainly grown under irrigation during winter (May to August).
Given this significant investment, wheat is mainly produced by medium and large-scale commercial farmers.
The introduction of a government subsidy from 2019 has maintained the production area above 40 000 ha with a further increase forecasted due to improved irrigation infrastructure.
However, only a few cultivars were widely adopted and grown by farmers (Table 2.1).
Wheat production in Zimbabwe is frequently affected by leaf rust due to the moist and hot environmental conditions at the beginning of the summer season.
In neighbouring SA, virulence of Pt has been monitored annually since the early 1980s (Pretorius and Le Roux, 1988).
Although the two countries share a border, it is crossed daily and therefore poses a high-risk of human, as well as windborne urediniospore dispersal between the two countries.
In this study a survey, which involves the collection of Pt infected wheat samples from the main wheat production regions of Zimbabwe, was conducted.
These isolates were also genotyped using microsatellite markers to determine the genetic relationships amongst Pt isolates from the two countries.
Thus, the aim of this study was to determine the diversity and distribution of Pt races in Zimbabwe during the 2019 to 2021 wheat production seasons.
Field isolates of Pt were collected through sampling of infected leaves from individual wheat cultivars in either commercial planting or trial plots.
Leaves were placed in a paper envelope labelled with the locality, wheat variety, leaf rust incidence in the commercial field or nursery and date of collection.
At least 2-3 leaves were sampled per plot of each sampled variety.
The envelopes were left open to air-dry at room temperature for 48 h before sealing.
Seedlings were fertilized once with 2.5 mg/L Multifeed-Classic water-soluble fertilizer [Effekto®, NPK Analysis 19:8:16 (43)] prior to inoculation.
Inoculations were carried out in an enclosed booth, which was cleaned through automated spraying of hot water (±65°C) for 60 s between isolates.
After inoculation, the seedlings were dried in a Conviron growth cabinet fitted with fluorescent growth tubes (200 μE/m2/s light) at 25°C for about 1 hour.
Inoculated seedlings were then incubated overnight (±18 h) in a dew simulation chamber at 19°C (±1°C).
Dew was formed by vapour released from two water baths at ±40°C fixed at the bottom of the chamber.
From the dew chamber, the seedlings were dried again in the Conviron growth cabinets for at least 2 h as described above before transferring them to the greenhouse.
Each pot was placed in a separate compartment in the greenhouse to prevent cross-contamination between isolates.
After 12 days, two single pustules were collected from each field isolate using a CHARACTERISATION OF Pt ISOLATES 44 vacuum connected spore collector.
Single pustule isolates were multiplied in a second round of inoculation of Morocco seedlings as described above.
The differential lines were planted in clusters (5 to 8 seeds per entry) following a circular pattern in 10 cm diameter pots filled with Mikskaar potting soil.
Five pots were placed per 30 cm diameter plastic tray to allow watering from below.
After planting, seeds were germinated at 25°C in a growth chamber for three days before placement under lights in a rust-free greenhouse cubicle at 18-25°C.
Seedlings were fertilized with 100 ml per tray of a 2.5 mg/L Multifeed-Classic water-soluble fertilizer [Effekto®, NPK Analysis 19:8:16 (43)].
Seven-day old seedlings of the differential lines having a fully developed primary leaf were inoculated with each isolate as previously described (2.2.2).
Seedlings were transplanted into 2 L pots filled with sterilized soil and grown in a greenhouse at ±21°C.
Plants were incubated in the dark in a dew chamber at ±19°C for 18 h as previously described above.
After the dew cycle, plants were dried at 20°C before moving them to a greenhouse cubicle set at an 18-25°C night/day schedule.
Leaf rust flag leaf response types were recorded 12 days after inoculation for each of the lines.
The same scale was applied 14 days after inoculation of the flag leaves to assess ITs of the differential lines carrying APR sources to Pt.
Infection types “0” to “2+” and combinations thereof were considered avirulent or low (L) for a particular Lr gene and ITs 3 to 4 as virulent or high (H).
Once seedling ITs were determined, a corresponding Pt letter code was assigned to the four-letter IT pattern.
The collection equipment was sterilized with 70% (v/v) ethanol between each sample to prevent contamination.
The samples were placed in 2 ml Eppendorf tubes and kept on ice for the duration of the sampling before being stored in a freezer at -80°C.
Two sterile 5 mm stainless steel balls were added to each 2 ml Eppendorf tube containing freeze-dried leaf samples.
The samples were ground to a fine powder using Qiagen’s TissueLyser (Haan, Germany) for 1 min at 30 r/s.
Samples were incubated for 1 h at 65°C and inverted every 15 minutes.
After discarding the supernatant, the DNA pellet was washed once with 500 µl ice-cold 70% (v/v) ethanol for 20 min at room temperature.
After centrifugation for 5 min at 12 000 g at 4°C the supernatant was discarded, and the DNA pellet air-dried for 1 h at room temperature.
The pellet was finally dissolved overnight at 4°C in 200 µl TE buffer (10 mM Tris-HCI, 1 mM EDTA pH 8.0).
RNA was removed from the extracted DNA by adding 2 µl RNase A (10 mg/ml) to each sample and incubating the tubes for 2 h at 37°C.
The supernatant was transferred to a new 1.5 ml Eppendorf tube and the DNA precipitated overnight at -20°C with 500 µl ice-cold 100% (v/v) ethanol.
Thereafter, the DNA samples were diluted to a working concentration of 10 ng/µl using water.
Gels were visualized and photographed using the Gel Doc™ EZ Imager (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, California, USA).
Each 10 µl PCR reaction contained 10 ng DNA, 1 µM of each primer set and a 1x concentration of KapaTaq Ready-mix (Sigma-Aldrich, USA).
A data matrix based on allele size was prepared for each dikaryotic individual.
To evaluate the extent of clonal reproduction, the presence of identical MLGs within the isolates, was recorded.
Clonal MLGs containing more than one isolate or race, were reduced to a single representative individual for further analysis.
A new allelic data set was thus created containing data for just these MLGs.
The minimal amount of valid data per marker was set at 70%, and 30 000 bootstraps were used to create the unrooted phylogram.
Clustering of individuals and the preparation of graphs were done within the ADEGENET webserver (Available from https://github.com/thibautjombart/adegenet).
The significance level of both the AMOVA components and the F-statistics parameter FST were tested using a total of 16 000 permutations.
The interpretation of an FST value above 0.15 was that there was a highly significant genetic discrimination between clusters (Wright, 1951).
The pairwise comparison between clusters as revealed by STRUCTURE analysis was also tested with AMOVA within ARLEQUIN version 3.5.1.2 at the 0.05 significance level.
Using this data set, a dendrogram was constructed using the unweighted NJ cluster analysis within DARwin version 5.0.158 (Perrier and Jacquemoud-Collet, 2006).
Possible correlation between the MLG phenotypic dendrogram and genotypic phylogram was calculated using the Mantel test within GenAIEX 6.5 (Peakall and Smouse, 2006; 2012) using the respective distance matrices.

Low rainfall between the 2017 to 2019 summer seasons resulted in low water reserves for wheat irrigation in the winter season.
This, coupled with frequent power cuts, forced most commercial farmers to reduce their wheat hectarage.
Furthermore, the land used for growing wheat during the winter seasons is far less than that of maize during the rain-fed summer season.
For example, wheat was grown on 50 000 ha during the 2019 winter season compared to 1.4 M ha of maize in the summer season.
So, currently wheat in Zimbabwe is grown on a small area compared to its potential.
These included Pt races, which emerged either through stepwise mutation of local races or through exotic introductions from other countries.

This gene is present on the 1B/1R wheat-rye translocation which is common in wheat lines developed by the CIMMYT based in México (Liu and Chen, 2012).
In addition, the variety turnover in Zimbabwe has been very low and dominated by only a few cultivars.
From 2019 to 2021, two new cultivars, SC Select and Peregrine, were also widely adopted and grown.
These cultivars were developed from crosses with lines developed by CIMMYT suggesting that they may also have the Lr26 gene.
The Lr37 gene is present in a small translocation from T. ventricosum Ces.
These provinces are directly adjacent to each other with no significant geographical barriers between them.
Population size also influences gene diversity through gene drift, in which a large population will more likely cause potential new mutations compared to smaller populations (McDonald and Linde, 2002).
This might aid in explaining the unique case of the dominance of race MCDS in Zimbabwe.
Other worldwide populations of Pt also have these characteristics where clonal reproduction is found (Kolmer, 2015).
The genetic relatedness of isolates from the different countries indicates the possible dispersal of fungal spores across the SADC region by wind, human activities, or other mechanisms.
Three variants of stem rust caused by Pgt race Ug99, namely TTKSF, PTKST and TTKSF+ were first detected in SA in 2000, 2009 and 2010, respectively.
A single pustule of Pt can produce around 2000 urediniospores per day for two weeks or more, thereby increasing the chances of mutations causing genetic variation.
Therefore, with a recent increase in hectarage and the expected release of new cultivars, we predict the evolution of more races of Pt in Zimbabwe.
This indicated that Ug99 arose by somatic hybridisation and nuclear exchange between an African member of the Pgt 21 lineage and an unknown isolate.
Thus, nuclear exchanges between dikaryotic fungi can contribute to the emergence of new virulent phenotypes with significant epidemiological impacts.
These genetic variations could have arisen due to either asexual recombination, single step mutations, somatic hybridisation or through new foreign introductions.
It is therefore important to broaden the genetic base by introducing new cultivars with a different combination of ASR and APR Lr genes.

Disease resistance has been the most effective method of controlling wheat leaf rust because it constitutes an environmentally friendly and cost-effective long-term strategy for minimising yield losses (Pink, 2002).
Resistance to wheat leaf rust is mainly divided into vertical and horizontal resistance (Yuan, 1998).
Vertical resistance, also known as race-specific or ASR, is often controlled by a single major gene and expressed throughout all plant growth stages.
Therefore, to reduce the risk of continuous boom-and-bust cycles, effective resistance genes need to be combined against the prevailing Pt race(s) to ensure longer lasting resistance.
Before gene pyramiding is carried out, it is important to identify effective and genetically different sources of resistance.
In this method, a host variety is evaluated against a collection of Pt isolates carrying different avirulence/virulence profiles based on phenotypic expressions in the form of seedling ITs (Kolmer, 2003).
Low ITs or resistant responses occur only when a wheat variety has a gene which conditions resistance to Pt races with the corresponding avirulence gene.
All-stage resistance genes are considered of lesser use when deployed singly in high-risk wheat production regions but remain useful when deployed in combination with other resistance genes.
Molecular markers closely linked to resistance genes have been developed to facilitate expeditious pyramiding into elite backgrounds, making it more cost- effective and less time-consuming.
This approach overcomes some of the problems associated with traditional gene postulation, such as gene interactions and plant stage of gene expression.
Most of them are ASR genes that confer hypersensitive reactions and interact with the pathogen in a gene-for-gene manner.
Therefore, stacking Lr genes into a single variety is considered a useful strategy as the combined effects of these genes give the variety a wider base of disease resistance.
There is not much information available in Zimbabwe on the Lr genes present in the released wheat varieties.
Similarly, we lack information on the identity and number of Lr genes present in advanced breeding lines of the SeedCo breeding programmes.
This study was therefore designed to identify ASR and APR genes in 72 Zimbabwean wheat entries that include advanced breeding lines from SeedCo as well as selected commercial varieties.
Gene postulation efforts included screening with multiple Pt races, pedigree analysis via F2 segregation ratios and molecular marker genotyping to effectively improve the accuracy of Lr gene identification.
These lines were selected from a F7 nursery, naturally infected with leaf rust (unknown race) during the 2019 season, where they expressed moderate to high levels of field resistance.
In addition, their grain yield performance, relative to commercial checks currently grown in Zimbabwe, was considered in the selection.
The 65 SeedCo varieties were bred from diverse backgrounds with some varieties sharing common parentage.
Varieties used in this study were therefore developed from the preceding stem rust resistance project.
Group 5 consisted of seven non SeedCo commercial varieties with unknown pedigrees.
Fresh inoculum was obtained by multiplying urediniospores on the universal susceptible variety Morocco.
Ten to twelve days after inoculation, primary leaf ITs were recorded according to the 0 to 4 seedling ITs scale (Table 3.2).
Heterogeneity on a leaf not adequately described with X, Y or Z may be written as a sequence, for example 12-.
The trial was set up in the second week of June by planting the wheat entries in observation rows that were 80 cm apart and 50 cm inter-row spacing.
The first application was done at four weeks and second application at eight weeks after crop emergence, regular irrigation was applied.
The trial was planted annually during the first week of June with trial entries planted in 1 m observation rows.
Leaf samples obtained from trial entries were utilised to confirm the Pt race dominated by natural infection.
At flowering a single ear from each of the selected Zimbabwean lines was crossed with a single ear of PAN 3497 pre-emasculated and covered with glycine crossing bags.
At flowering the ears from each pot were covered with pollination bags LEAF RUST RESISTANCE 90 (CCR Stitchworx Products, Potchefstroom, SA) to prevent cross-pollination.
Upon ripening, the F2 seeds were bulked from the 10 plants per cross and hand threshed.
Six pots were placed per 30 cm diameter plastic tray to allow watering from below.
The parents used in each crossing combination were planted in replicate as controls and added as a seventh pot to each tray.
After planting, seeds were germinated at 25°C in a growth chamber for three days before placement under natural light in a rust-free greenhouse cubicle at 18-25°C (night/day cycle).
Seedlings were fertilised twice with 100 ml of a 2.5 mg/L Multifeed-Classic water-soluble fertilizer (3.2.5.1) per tray, once prior and once post inoculation.
Seven-day old seedlings, with a fully developed primary leaf, were inoculated with freshly collected urediniospores from Pt race MCDS (ZIM isolate Pt1_1_2019).
Leaf samples were collected in 1.5 ml Eppendorf tubes and stored on ice during sample collection.
Samples were incubated for 1 h at 65°C with regular light shaking.
Thereafter, 200 µl/ml RNase was added to each sample and incubated for 2 h in a water bath at 37°C to digest the RNA.
Using a Jenway 7315 spectrophotometer (Jenway, Staffordshire, UK), the absorbance was measured at A260, A280, and the A260:280 ratios to calculate the DNA concentration for each sample.

Twenty-one of the 25 varieties selected for outcrosses showed fleck IT responses to all nine Pt pathotypes, except for SC003, SC038, SC047 and SC050 (Table 3.6).
The fleck response to all nine Pt pathotypes was consistent with the presence of Lr19 and Lr47 in the differential lines.

According to molecular marker data, three outcrosses carried Lr9 and 20 carried Lr19.
Genes Lr11, Lr50 and Lr51 were also detected by molecular markers in ten, six and twenty-four of the outcrosses respectively (Table 3.9).
The presence of Lr9, Lr11, Lr50 and Lr51 in the tested varieties was therefore questionable based on the observed discrepancies.
All seven outcrosses from group 3 from the Lr19/Sr25 background were confirmed to carry Lr19 as expected.
The presence of APR genes was masked by ASR genes present in each of these entries under field conditions.

The Lr34/Yr18/Sr57 gene was not present in any of the varieties used in outcrosses but was present in two varieties namely SC033 and Peregrine.

This questions the presence of these genes in the rest of the varieties based on molecular marker data.
However, MAS was not applied to confirm if the successful introgression of these genes and selection were based on field responses following natural infection from uncharacterised Pt isolates.

The remaining varieties where low and high seedling IT patterns were recorded either carried unique genes not present, or gene combinations not accounted for, in the 46 differential lines.

These results therefore indicated to Lr19 as the single inherited dominant gene.
Furthermore, Lr19 was previously not detected in SC Nduna and SC Shungu.
Groups 1 and 3 that had Sr25 parentage background contributed 12 outcrosses carrying Lr19, while group 4 had eight outcrosses with Lr19 as expected from their known pedigrees.
Other ASR genes detected by molecular markers (Lr9, Lr11, Lr26, Lr29, Lr50 and Lr51) had low to intermediate (; to 2+) to high (Lr26) IT responses.
The Lr26 gene was not effective against the confirmed dominant Pt race MCDS.
Two varieties used in outcrosses, LEAF RUST RESISTANCE 121 SC003 and SC038, deviated from the fleck IT response and showed MR field responses at Greytown.
Based on the false positives observed for Lr11 and Lr51, it is also possible that they carry unique ASR genes.
An MR response in the field was therefore expected due to their none-immune responses at seedling stage.
Since assayed markers still recombine with the target gene, this disparity is proportional to their distance from the target locus.
To limit the influence of recombination, it is consequently required to rely on at least a few markers flanking the target locus/QTL.
In this instance, it is possible to forecast the frequency of false positives using the product of the distances between the two markers flanking the targeted locus.
To achieve this, the gene of interest is cloned either by positional cloning or functional examination of candidate genes in the locus region and the desired polymorphisms are identified.
Thus, it is possible to design the so-called ‘perfect marker’ that is not subjected to recombination.
The Lr9 gene was detected in six varieties of which three has been confirmed as likely false positives through outcrosses.
The gene encodes an unusual tandem kinase fusion protein, a trait important in disease resistance.
The Lr11 gene was detected in 22 varieties, which showed several responses.
They displayed either uncharacteristic low (fleck) and high (≥3) ITs in the greenhouse and R and MR responses in field trials.
Previous studies on Zimbabwean germplasm did not report the presence of Lr11.
However, there is no evidence to support that this was a consequence of the use of Lr11 in local varieties in these countries.
Similarly, Lr19/Sr25 has been used in Australia, Egypt, Pakistan, Afghanistan and CIMMYT breeding programmes.
Forty varieties were confirmed to carry Lr19 using markers Gb and PSY closely linked to Lr19/Sr25.
In our study, the STSLr24 marker did not detect the presence of Lr24 in any of the Zimbabwean wheat varieties.
In the Zimbabwean context, Lr24 can still be deployed since it is effective against the currently dominant Pt race MCDS.
The Lr26 gene was derived from rye and exists in bread wheat as the 1BL/1RS translocation.
In the current study, Lr26 was detected in 23 varieties using molecular markers.
The 1BL/1RS translocation is no longer effective to a wide range of Pt races.
Varieties SC044 and SC045 had low ITs (mostly flecks) similar to RL6080 (Lr29) for all the tested Pt races and showed resistance in all field trials.
This gene is a potential resistance source to new Pt races that might occur in Zimbabwe and neighbouring countries.
The gene has not been previously reported in the Zimbabwean wheat varieties.
The gene was predicted to occur in 13 varieties using flanking markers Gwm382 and Gdm87.
The variety K215W119 was clearly susceptible to some Pt race isolates and although SC048 produced low ITs similar to Lr50, it was also predicted to carry Lr51.
The presence of Lr50 in the current set of germplasm could not be confirmed.
The highest frequency of detected ASR genes by molecular markers, was Lr51, which was predicted to occur in 66 of the Zimbabwean varieties.
Unfortunately, these did include 21 likely false positives as predicted from the F2 segregation ratios.
However, its predicted presence in SC047 and SC050 needs confirmation as this is contradicted by their fleck low ITs.
The Lr51 gene was previously not commonly deployed in breeding programmes, despite the good levels of resistance it conferred, but can be useful in the SeedCo breeding programme.
The segregation results for the F2 populations revealed the presence of single dominant ASR genes in the majority of the populations fitting the theoretically expected ratios of 3:1.
However the presence of a single recessive gene was also revealed in a population from cross PAN3497/SC003 with a segregation ratio of 1:3.
The population from cross PAN3497/SC065 revealed the presence of two independent resistance genes.
The combination of several effective resistance genes into a single wheat LEAF RUST RESISTANCE 125 variety can extend the period of resistance against the development of new virulent races.
Molecular markers detected the presence of the ASR genes Lr11, Lr19 and Lr51.
Based on the ITs and pedigree background, Lr19 is highly likely to be one of the dominant genes, with either Lr11, Lr51 or an unknown gene, being the other.
The resistance phenotype displayed by this gene includes a longer latent period, fewer and smaller uredinia.
The Lr68 APR gene was detected in ten Zimbabwean wheat varieties which showed varying responses during greenhouse and field tests.
K215W119 with Lr68 in combination with Lr37 showed high ITs to isolates of Pt races MCDS, CBPS and MFPS in the greenhouse and a MRMS reaction type in the field.
For this study, Lr27 had the second highest frequency of APR genes in the 72 Zimbabwean varieties and was detected in 25 varieties.
Some lines from that study were used as parental lines to develop entries in group 2.
At present, Lr46 still maintains good resistance that makes it an ideal candidate to combine with other resistance genes to achieve durable leaf rust resistance.
The Lr46 gene was the most common APR source in the Zimbabwean wheat varieties and was detected in 33 varieties.
The Lr46 gene is the most utilised APR gene in the Zimbabwean breeding programmes, but its frequency can still be improved.
Only five varieties carried Lr37 in the tested panel of Zimbabwean varieties.
However, resistance donors known to carry Lr37 have not been extensively used in the Zimbabwean wheat breeding programme.
The stem rust variants of Ug99, namely TTKSF, TTKSF+ and PTKST previously reported in Zimbabwe, are virulent to Sr38 (Terefe, 2021).
A thorough analysis of the prevalence and distribution of both ASR and APR genes is necessary for the effective utilisation of genetic resistance to leaf rust.
Using F2 segregation ratios and molecular markers, Lr19 and five APR genes were detected in a collection of Zimbabwean wheat germplasm.
Additional sources of ASR may be present but could not be postulated, as most varieties carried ASR sources effective to all the Pt races.
Secondly the low and high IT patterns for most varieties did not match that of the single gene differential lines.
This indicated, although defeated in some, the presence of more complex sources of resistance in the Zimbabwean wheat collection.
The identified resistant varieties are a potential source of both ASR and APR Lr genes in Zimbabwe.
Results from this study confirmed that there is an overreliance on the Lr19 ASR and Lr46 and Lr27 APR genes.
Therefore, an urgent need to combine more APR genes and increase the frequency of Lr34 and Lr68, exists to extend the duration of leaf rust resistance.
The slow rusting Lr67 APR gene which was not detected in the current set needs to be incorporated in the Zimbabwean wheat breeding programmes to develop durable resistance.
The findings of this study emphasised the significance of APR genes in providing durable leaf rust resistance in wheat, as well as the necessity of gene pyramiding.

It ranks as the second most strategic food crop in Zimbabwe after maize with its main products being wheat flour and bran.
Wheat flour is the main ingredient for making bread and confectionaries, consumed by over eight million households daily (Zimstat, 2021).
Wheat bran is used for making stock feeds in the manufacturing sector.
Thus, the wheat industry in Zimbabwe contributes substantially to food security and employment.
Despite these socio-economic advantages, wheat production is still low due to unstable yields with the occurrence of diseases being one of the constraints.
An average annual production of approximately 200 000 tonnes from a cultivated area of 66 000 ha is insufficient to provide in the local demand.
Zimbabwe imports wheat to decrease the deficit of the required 450 000 tonnes per annum (Zimstat, 2021).
Among the biotic constraints of wheat production in Zimbabwe is the annual presence of one of the most commonly occurring fungal pathogens of wheat, Pt that causes leaf rust.
Most farmers rely on fungicides to protect susceptible varieties against the disease, thereby increasing the production cost.
The underlying importance of resistance to wheat leaf rust in commercial farming is continuously highlighted by the widespread use of fungicides.
However, planting resistant varieties can be equally efficient and more environmentally friendly to minimise losses.
This provides an opportunity to develop widely adapted high yielding and leaf rust resistant wheat varieties.
In Zimbabwe, farmers are interested in wheat varieties with stable high yield and good agronomic traits including early maturity, lodging tolerance and semi-dwarf types considering plant height.
The millers expect varieties with good milling qualities such as high flour yield, while the bakeries require varieties with good baking qualities such as strong flours with high gluten content.
Consumers prefer a good quality loaf consisting of a crispy crust, not too dense with a glossy interior and of good flavour.
To identify varieties that can meet these criteria, there is a need for METs across the main representative wheat growing regions of Zimbabwe.
Crop scientists focus on breeding, testing and selecting genotypes that show superior performance in different environments.
Cross-over interaction is whereby a genotype is superior in one environment but a poor performing genotype in another environment.
Inefficiency in GxE analysis can present problems to breeders and plant pathologists leading to wrong varietal recommendations.
Poor performing or unstable varieties can contribute to decreased food security in the long run.
Several statistical methods are available that can be used to understand GxE effects.
Moreover, the GGE analysis is an effective method which is based on the PCA to fully explore MET.
The aim of this chapter was to analyse multi-location and season trial data for 72 Zimbabwean wheat varieties to draw varietal recommendations for commercialisation.
These sites were selected based on the main commercial wheat production areas in Zimbabwe and are geographically located on the highveld (>1200 masl), and middleveld (800 to 1200 masl).
List of 72 Zimbabwean wheat varieties planted in multi-environment trials (METs) in Zimbabwe during 2020 and 2021.
Since plots were machine planted, the fine seedbed was required to provide an equal sowing depth and ease of movement of the machinery during planting.
The seeding rate was 120 kg/ha for all plots over two seasons.
The objective was to achieve a plant stand of 250 to 300 plants per m2.
In two split applications, ammonium nitrate (NH4NO3, 34.5% N) was utilised as a top-dressing fertiliser.
The first spray was made four to five weeks following crop emergence, and the second application was made six to eight weeks later.
Each plot received a hand-applied top dressing of fertiliser, which was immediately followed by a light (20 mm) irrigation.
Weed management was done by a combination of herbicides and hand weeding where necessary.
Aphids were controlled using Dimethoate where necessary, as recommended on the label, and bird scarers were engaged at all sites from grain filling up to harvesting.
Genotypes were planted in 10 rows 6 m in length with an inter-row spacing of 20 cm using a modified small plot tractor drawn seed drill.
Harvested grain was collected into 5 kg harvesting bags labelled with the plot numbers and trial site name.
Net plot yield: Harvested grain from each net plot was weighed using an electronic scale (DPYH Platform, Nicolas Scale, Harare, Zimbabwe) to determine the grain in kilograms.
The following important factors required by Zimbabwean millers and bakers were considered when interpreting the data from recording these variables.
Starch content (%): A trait that is normally not a primary quality trait in Zimbabwe during wheat trade, although ≥60% is considered desirable.
Test weight density (kg/hl): The minimum acceptable test weight density is 75 kg/hl.
The collected and derived data (yield and LRCI) was subjected to analysis of variance (ANOVA) to determine differences between means.
Fisher’s least significant difference (LSD) at 1% and 5% probability levels were used to separate the variable means of G, E and GxE.
To determine the general performance of an experimental genotype in relation to the optimum response averaged over all locations, the variety superiority measure (Pi) was calculated.
In addition, genotypes were ranked according to the mean performance at all the tested environments for each trait.
Pearson’s r correlation coefficient was used to test the relationship between variables.
No problems were experienced with germination and seedling establishment and the plant stand was maintained optimally throughout the two growing seasons.
No fungicides were sprayed to control fungal diseases to allow for natural occurrence and spread of Pt in the trials.
Natural appearance of leaf rust was observed annually in trials at the onset of flowering.
Mean values of the tested genotypes and the range of corresponding traits across the four tested environments are presented in Table 4.3.
The presence of the GxE was indicated by changes in mean rankings of genotypes for different traits over trial sites.
Significant differences between genotypes were observed for all the tested traits based on the LSD values at 0.05 significance level.
Similarly, all varieties met the minimum industry requirements for starch and test weight densities of 60% and 75 kg/hl respectively (Table 4.4).
Genotype, E and GxE were estimated by the additive main effect and AMMI model (Table 4.4).
The GxE effects contributed highly to the variance observed for LRCI and wet gluten.
The environment had greater effect on the variance in days to anthesis, grain protein content, starch and test weight density.
Means and ranks of agronomic and quality traits, and leaf rust response (LRCI) for 72 wheat varieties tested at four sites in Zimbabwe during the 2020 and 2021 growing seasons.
The variety superiority measure was computed to determine stable and superior varieties (Table 4.7).
With the CSI method, a genotype with the lowest CSI indicates the most stable and superior variety.
Variety SC001 was the highest yielding variety and MRI 834 was ranked lowest in grain yield.
Means of grain yield and variety superiority index (CSI) value for 72 wheat varieties tested at four sites in Zimbabwe during the 2020 and 2021 growing seasons.
The biplot explained 93.73% of the total variation observed, of which 83.43% was explained by the first principal component (PC1), while the second principal component explained 10.31%.
The polygon view showed that the panel of 72 test varieties were distributed across all the sectors.
The GGE-biplots demarcated environments into two major ME namely, ME1 and ME2.
Panmure was shown to be a unique environment further away from the other three.
Genotypes G72, G69, G67, G71, G25 and G66 fell in sectors with no defined environmental conditions, indicating poor adaptation to the ME.
The yield performance of genotypes is determined by the length of the abscissa where above average is on the right and below average on the left.
Greater absolute length of the ordinate of a genotype indicates lower stability with more variability and shorter length indicates higher stability and less variability.
FIELD AND QUALITY TRAITS EVALUATION 159 4.3.7 Pearson’s r correlation coefficients among tested agronomic traits Pearson’s r correlation coefficients among agronomic- and quality traits were studied.
Strong negative correlations (P ≤ 0.001), were revealed between protein content and starch (-0.85) and between wet gluten and starch (- 0.82).
Analysis further revealed moderate but significantly negative correlations (P ≤ 0.001), between leaf rust response and grain yield (-0.43) as well as days to anthesis (-0.34).
Protein content was negatively correlated to yield (-0.10) although not significant (P > 0.05).
Starch content showed a small but significant positive correlation with grain yield (0.15; P ≤ 0.05).
However, there was no significant effect of the variety responses between leaf rust response and protein content (0.05) or starch content (-0.06) and test weight densities (0.09).
The small but significant positive correlation revealed between leaf rust response and wet gluten, indicate that varieties with higher LRCI values had higher gluten content.
In this study these effects were demonstrated by a change in genotype ranking across the trial sites for all seven traits.
From the analysis the GxE effects, although remaining significant, were lower than the effects of G and E, for all the traits.
Heritability for the traits analysed varied from moderate to high, ranging from 0.59 to 0.9.
This implies that more than half of the differences observed for LRCI, days to anthesis, protein and starch content, test weight density and wet gluten content are from genetic factors.
Heritability data assists plant breeders to predict the behaviour of the succeeding generation and increase the chance of making desirable selections.
The higher the heritability for a trait, the more straightforward the selection process and the greater the response to selection.
Grain yield is a quantitative trait which significantly interacts with the environment.
Hence, the selection of the best performing varieties with wider adaptability is a cumbersome task.
GGE-biplot analysis assists in selecting the best and most stable performing genotypes in MET (Yan and Tinker, 2006).
For effective interpretation of a GGE-biplot, the ‘which-won-where’ model also termed as polygon view, is quite handy as it depicts interaction patterns between environments and genotypes (Yan and Kang, 2003).
This view, in combination with the mean genotype ranking and CSI, clearly demonstrated that the top five high yielding and stable varieties are SC001, SC002, SC004, SC0027 and SC W9101.
Varieties SC041 and SC043 were also high yielding and stable across environments but with their grain protein content below the required 11%, cannot be selected as ideal varieties.
The GGE scatter plot grouped the four environments into two MEs where ART Farm (environment 2) had the highest mean grain yield and Panmure (environment 4) the lowest.
In this case, ART Farm can represent ME 1 and Panmure can represent ME 2.
However, this was accompanied by non-significant correlations between LRCI and protein and starch content, test weight density as well as wet gluten content.
This can be explained by 51 of the 72 varieties with low LRCI values (≤5) indicating strong resistance responses.
Only ten of the 72 varieties had LRCI values between 42 and 70 indicating moderate susceptibility to Pt.
From these five varieties namely SC Shungu, MRI 834, SST 875, Peregrine and SC042 were also early flowering with low mean yield performances.
A significant negative correlation was also observed between LRCI and days to anthesis.
High yielding varieties in this study were mostly medium to late flowering, which explains the small but significant positive correlation between anthesis and yield performance.
It was therefore not surprising to observe a strong and significant negative correlation between starch with both protein and wet gluten content.
Similarly, a small but significant negative correlation was observed between yield and wet gluten content although the similar small negative correlation between yield and protein content was not significant.
Negative correlations between yield and test weight density are often influenced by stress factors occurring during the grain-filling period resulting in lower hectolitre mass.
These stressors could include drought, excessive soil moisture, a shortage of nutrients, too little sunlight and too low or too high temperatures (Johansson, 2002).
The results showed a significant positive correlation between wet gluten and grain protein content.
This positive association was expected since the influence of protein content on wet gluten is well known.
This indicates that MAS for Glu-B3 can be useful in selecting genotypes with desirable protein and wet gluten content.
In this study we observed that the early flowering variety MRI 834 with moderate susceptibility to Pt in combination with a low yield had higher protein and wet gluten content.
The small but significant positive correlation between LRCI with both gluten and protein content cannot be attributed to Pt infection only.
Early flowering accompanied by low yield also appear to be contributing factors, especially considering that most genotypes in the current study were resistant to leaf rust.
Leaf rust disease resulted in lower yield and test weight densities, as low-test weight densities result in lower endosperm to bran ratio (Dimmock and Gooding, 2002).
Therefore, it is expected that a leaf rust susceptible variety would have higher protein concentration from bran but with low yield due to shrivelled grain affected by the disease.
This could aid in explaining the high protein content observed in MRI 834 which is moderately susceptible, early flowering and low yielding.
The reasons might be that the disease came in or peaked late during grain filling with minimum effect on the test weight densities, protein and starch content.
Furthermore, irrigation allowing for sufficient moisture also limited the stress caused by late disease infection.
A shortcoming of the current study is that a leaf rust check variety like PAN 3497 or SC Shine was not included in the trials.
Grain quality is important as it defines the end-use of wheat and contributes to maximise profit across the wheat value chain.
It adds value to the rest of the breeding activities as it is a key set of characteristics for the commercialisation and trading of wheat.
Grain quality should form an integral part of the breeding process and be considered within the variety development process.
In breeding programmes, end-use quality phenotyping is laborious, expensive, time- consuming and can require a large amount of grain.
In contrast to single-locus molecular markers, GS can capture the genetic complexity of the different quality traits at once, thus making the selection process more efficient and accurate.
It is thus a recommended method for adoption by Zimbabwean researchers in future.
In conclusion, this study showed that grain yield and quality traits were determined mainly by E effects followed by G influence.
The observed negative association between high yield and some quality traits should be an important target for future breeding efforts in Zimbabwe.
Furthermore, although showing high yield performance in field trials, variety SC001 is not a good choice for release as it carries no known APR genes.
Therefore, there is a need to introgress a combination of effective ASR and APR genes into new wheat varieties.

The 46 differential lines and nine Pt races used did not allow gene postulation for any ASR genes.

Twenty-three of the 25 varieties selected for outcrossing displayed an F2 segregation ratio of 3:1, indicating the inheritance of a single dominant gene.
These results point to the presence of Lr19 as the singly inherited ASR gene dominant in SeedCo germplasm.
Furthermore, the pedigree information based on the previous genotypic results for Sr25, with a tight linkage to Lr19, was predictive of the findings.
Groups 1 and 3 with Sr25 parentage background contributed 12 outcrosses carrying Lr19, while group 4 had eight outcrosses with Lr19 as expected from their known pedigrees.

Previous studies have suggested that the linkage between flanking markers and the gene of interest is not complete compared to diagnostic markers developed from cloned genes.
Hence the occurrence of false positives when using flanking markers is expected in different genetic backgrounds.
Nevertheless, Lr gene flanking markers can be used effectively in a marker- assisted backcrossing programme in conjunction with regular phenotypic monitoring if satisfactory parental genotypes are to be selected.
Findings from this study have shown that Zimbabwean and SeedCo breeding programmes rely heavily on the monogenic resistance of Lr19.
The deployment of a combination of Lr19 with APR genes in a single variety is therefore highly recommended.
Five APR genes (Lr27, Lr34, Lr37, Lr46 and Lr68) were detected in the Zimbabwean germplasm, with Lr46 being the most common among them and Lr34 the least common.
Therefore, an urgent need exists to increase the frequency of Lr34 and find sources carrying Lr67 for use in the SeedCo wheat breeding programmes.

The disease was more prevalent in Sindh and Punjab than other parts, with little infestation in the northern cold wheat growing regions.
Among the major cultivated varieties surveyed, severe infestation was observed for wheat varieties Galaxy-2013, Morocco, TD_1, Sehar, Yecora, Aas-11, Inqilab-91, Kiran-95, Shafaq, Sarsabz, TJ-83, Marvi, Sassi and some local lines.

Despite of this intense importance, the average yield of wheat per hectare is much lesser than progressive countries (Brian, 2006).

Many challenges are faced by farmers to achieve high yields of wheat including biotic and abiotic factors.
Annual yield losses in China by leaf rust are estimated at three million tons.
Although in Pakistan the disease onset is delayed in the northern part, its onset is regular in the major wheat growing region of Punjab.
Climatic changes and subsequent variability in crop duration require rigorous wheat leaf rust surveillance to keep an eye on the disease and its emergence in previously unaffected areas.
Thus, the present study was designed to assess the countrywide situation of leaf rust in different geographical and climatic situation with the response of host to disease.
Considering the aerial dispersal of leaf rust pathogens, an attempt was made to cover the maximum area of the representative wheat growing region.
After every 10 to 20 kilometers depending on presence of wheat fields, surveillance was conducted.
To score host response to infection, the infection types was measured (Singh, 1993).
The host reaction types in the order of R (resistance), MR (moderately resistant), MRMS (moderately resistant-moderately susceptible), MS (moderately susceptible) and S (susceptible) was recorded.
Analyses of surveillance data and average coefficient of infection (ACI): The surveillance data was analysed in MS Excel and in R-statistical environment.
The geographical distribution of the leaf rust across various geographical locations and different hosts was analysed based on its relative prevalence as a function of geography and host.
Average coefficient of infection was calculated by multiplying disease severity and an incrimental value for each infection types (Pathan & Park, 2007; Saari & Wilcoxson, 1974).
The numbers of districts and wheat fields surveyed in different provinces varied in each year of surveillance, depending on the availability of wheat crop in the region.
Leaf rust prevailed in most of the areas during 2017 while in 2016 and 2018 relatively low disease pressure was recorded.
A total of 69 fields with high disease pressure were recorded across country during three years.
In case of varieties surveyed over multiple locations, the response of the host to leaf rust varied across locations.
Galaxy-13 was recorded with high disease severity at most locations surveyed (KP, Sindh and Punjab).
A high disease was also observed on Sehar in Sindh and Punjab.

The present study enabled to identify the countrywide distribution of leaf rust across Pakistan.
Leaf rust prevailed at most of the areas of Sindh, southern Punjab and some parts of KP and northern Punjab.
The high leaf rust prevalence in Sindh and southern Punjab may be attributed to warm environmental conditions of those areas (Khalil & Jan, 2003).
Certain leaf rust resistance genes are temperature sensitive especially high temperatures, while some leaf rust resistance (Lr) gene expression is also halted at lower temperatures (Dyck & Johnson, 1983).
Change of temperature during early penetration phase alters the host- pathogen interaction (Hyde, 1982).
Most of the Lr genes are affected by post infection temperatures; where Lr11, Lr12, Lr13, Lr14a, Lr16, Lr17 and Lr18 are particularly sensitive to high temperature (Dyck & Johnson, 1983).
For leaf rust most of major varieties grown in southern country showed susceptible reaction.
The susceptibility of major wheat varieties to leaf rust can be due to the presence of virulence against the Lr genes or down expression of Lr genes at higher temperatures.

Yellow rust, caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici, is a significant wheat disease worldwide.
In Latvia, the distribution of yellow rust has increased recently and new aggressive races have been identified.
The aim of this research was to investigate the possibilities for the biological control of yellow rust in winter wheat.
A field trial was established in a biological field of winter wheat in Latvia in 2017 and 2018.
Biological products that contained Bacillus spp., Pseudomonas aurantiaca, Brevibacillus spp., Acinetobacter spp., and chitosan were used for treatments, and one variant was left untreated.
The efficacy of products was evaluated by the AUDPC (area under the disease progress curve) comparison.
Differences in the severity of yellow rust between the trial years were observed.
After two years of investigations, the results were not convincing; therefore, further research is needed.

Seedling tests with multiple Puccinia triticina (Pt) pathotypes indicated the presence of seedling genes Lr13 (in both ‘Spark’ and ‘Rialto’) and Lr26 (‘Rialto’).
Composite interval mapping indicated involvement of consistent QTLs on chromosomes 3AS (QLr.sun-3AS), 3BS (QLr.sun-3BS) and 4D (QLr.sun-4D) across all environments.
QTLs QLr.sun-3AS and QLr.sun-4D were contributed by Rialto and QLr.sun- 3BS was contributed by Spark.
Initially, QLr.sun-3BS was thought to be associated with a QTL for stem rust resistance, and was therefore selected for further fine mapping.
To saturate this region, 40 new SSR, STS, DArT markers and 17 SNP markers were tested.
The results validated the potential use of these tightly linked markers to QLr.sun-3BS in marker-assisted breeding.
A request has been lodged for a permanent locus designation for LrSpa in accordance with the rules of wheat gene nomenclature.
With the absence of Sr31 virulence in the field, the QTL QSr.sun-1BS was attributed to the seedling resistance gene Sr31.
These markers should be very useful for further refining the map and in marker assisted selection.
Greenhouse seedling tests against eight Pst pathotypes indicated the presence of five known genes (Yr3, Yr4, Yr6, Yr7 and Yr9) and uncharacterised seedling resistance (USR) to Pst.
In the field, the parents and all the DH lines displayed high levels of resistant, giving “0” to “TR” infection types.
No susceptible segregants were observed against field Pst pathotypes across all data sets, in which both the parents displayed high levels of resistance.
Genotyping of the DH population using the Yr4-linked marker barc75 revealed the presence of Yr4 in Rialto and 41 DH lines.
In field tests, all three populations showed a satisfactory fit to a 7:8:1 ratio, suggesting that two genes were involved in controlling stripe rust resistance.
Of these two genes, one is a seedling resistance gene (either YrSpa, Yr3 or Yr4) and the second an uncharacterised APR.

In field tests, 19 (24%) genotypes were susceptible, whereas 50 (64%) genotypes gave highly to moderately resistant responses to leaf rust.
Field tests at adult plant growth stage indicated that six (8%) genotypes were susceptible.

Three (4%) genotypes displayed moderate levels of resistance and the remaining 66 (85%) genotypes were highly resistant.

Wheat is believed to have originated in southwestern Asia (Gibson and Benson 2002), with some of the earliest remains of the crop being found in Syria, Jordan, and Turkey.
It is one of the main staple foods in both developed and developing countries.
Wheat is an important crop in many developing countries, both in production and consumption.
Crop production throughout the world is reduced significantly by biotic and abiotic stresses.
Biotic stresses like diseases, insects and weeds can destroy between 31 to 42% of all crops annually (Agrios 2005).
Approximately 14% of these losses are due to diseases, which amount to about US$220 billion per year (Agrios 2005).
Likewise, wheat is attacked by pathogens such as parasitic fungi, viruses, bacteria, and nematodes, all capable of reducing yield significantly.
The rust diseases are caused by fungi belonging to the class Basidiomycetes and order Pucciniales.
The rust fungi are highly specialised pathogens with significant variation for avirulence/virulence to specific host resistance genes.
Rust pathogens differ in morphology, life cycle and environmental preferences for growth and development.
Pgt develops well under hot and humid conditions, while Pst prefers a cooler climate.
These pathogens are also the most serious problems contributing to low productivity of cereal crops in eastern Africa, including Ethiopia.
In Australia, wheat production has been threatened by stem rust virtually since European settlement in the late 18th Century (McIntosh and Brown 1997).
Effective control of cereal rust diseases is possible mainly through utilisation of genetic resistance to the pathogen, and fungicides (Brennan and Quade 2004b).
On the other hand, annual savings from chemical sprays were valued at approximately AUD $12 million across the three rusts.
Under lower yielding and low return systems, resistance genes offer the most cost effective approach to control rust diseases in wheat (Park 2008).
In both cases, the selection of virulent pathotypes is accelerated if large areas are planted to a single variety (Roelfs 1985).
This helps to ensure the cultivars in farmers’ fields have effective genetic resistance against current rust pathotypes and prevents the increase of rust pathogen populations.
Bearing these points in mind, the current study is focused on the following objectives: 1.
Characterisation and molecular mapping of leaf rust resistance in the European winter wheat cultivars Spark and Rialto 2.
Characterisation and mapping of resistance loci against Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici in European winter wheat cultivars Spark and Rialto 3.
Identification and characterisation of stripe rust resistance genes in European winter wheat cultivars Spark and Rialto 4.
The minimum, optimum and maximum temperatures for wheat growth are 3°C to 4°C, 25°C, 30°C to 32°C, respectively (Briggle 1980).
It is adapted to a broad range of moisture conditions, from xerophytic to littoral (Curtis 2002).
Wheat is often classified into spring and winter types to indicate the season during which it is grown.
Heading is late in winter wheat, and requires a period of cold temperatures.
A large amount of wheat is utilised within the country where it is produced and only one-fifth of the annual crop is exported.
To tackle this challenge, understanding the structure and function of the wheat genome is essential.
It has the largest genome at 16,000 Mb, about eight times larger than the maize genome and 40 times larger than that of rice (Arumuganathan and Earle 1991).
A core feature of great significance in relation to the distribution and epidemiology of the cereal rusts is their plasticity.
There are more than 7,000 rust species that attack many plant species (McKenzie 1998).
In the past, stem rust was potentially the most feared disease of wheat, damaging crops periodically on a massive scale.
Where environmental conditions are suitable for rust development, total yield loss is likely to occur on susceptible cultivars (Hodson 2011).
To a large extent, cereal rust research has been one of challenge and response.
The most noticeable structures of the wheat rust pathogens visible to the naked eye are the uredinial and telial stages.
Taxonomy and nomenclature Rust fungi belong to the class Basidiomycetes and the order Pucciniales.
The absence of clamp connections is an important characteristic that differentiates the Pucciniales from other members of the Basidiomycota.
Rust fungi that produce all five spore forms (sometimes excluding pycniospores) are termed macrocyclic.
Such species can be autoecious, (limited to a single host) or heteroecious, (attacking alternate hosts) (Petersen 1974).
The second life cycle in rust fungi, in which a uredinial stage (and sometimes the pycnial stage) is lacking, is called demicyclic.
While demicyclic rusts may be either autoecious or heteroecious, microcyclic forms are necessarily aoutoecious due to the short life cycle (Petersen 1974).
When individuals are produced asexually, the frequency and degree of variability among progeny are reduced greatly but even then certain individuals may show different characteristics.
To know how host resistance genes are overcome by pathogens, we need to understand the process of pathogen evolution.
Research to date has indicated that the following mechanisms lead to rust pathogens overcoming the resistance of cultivars: (a) mutation to virulence, (b) sexual recombination, (c) asexual recombination (Kiyosawa 1982).
Mechanisms of variablity Mutation: Mutation is the ultimate source of new alleles in plant pathogens, being the most common process that diversifies pathogen variability within a short period (CIMMYT 1988).
According to the gene-for-gene hypothesis (Flor 1971), elicitor molecules produced by pathogens are recognised by specific receptors in the plant.
When a pathogen elicitor is recognised by a plant cell receptor, a defense mechanism is activated enhancing hypersensitive cell death of the infected plant and restricting pathogen growth.
Host resistance “breakdown” is therefore due to a change in the pathogen from avirulence to virulence (McDonald and Linde 2002).
In order to infect a variety having two or more resistance genes, the pathogen must have virulence on all resistance genes present in the host (Flor 1971).
Mutation provides the basic variation that occurs in rust pathogens (Roelfs 1985).
In Australia, pathogenic variation in cereal rusts occurs principally via mutation (McIntosh 1992b).
Selection: Selection is one of the normal evolutionary forces that determine phenotypic variability of rust pathogen populations in adverse environments (McIntosh and Brown 1997).
These pathotypes could not attack most of the wheat cultivars in the areas where they occurred, but were selected for on triticales with corresponding resistance genes.
Generally, the host genotypes on which a rust pathogen survives between seasons will influence the genotypes of a pathogen that survive (CIMMYT 1988).
Sexual recombination: The presence of alternate hosts near wheat fields can create opportunities for the evolution of new rust pathotypes (Roelfs 1985).
In Australia, because barberry is not present, the evolution of new pathotypes has apparently resulted from mutation and somatic recombination (Luig and Watson 1972; Anikster and Wahl 1979).
Globally, the sexual stage of Pt is rarely found, and the alternate Thalictrum spp.
As a result, sexual reproduction in the pathogen is limited in nature.
Somatic hybridisation: Anastomosis of germ tubes and hyphae occurs readily in rust fungi, and it is reasonable to expect mitotic recombination to occur (Samborski 1985).
Somatic hybridisation involves exchange of nuclei between fusing hyphae in the dikaryotic stage (Park and Wellings 2012).
As a precondition, presence of congenial host is very important for the occurrence of somatic recombination.
Migration: Migration and dispersal are the main evolutionary strategies enabling organisms to colonise new areas.
The spores of many fungal pathogens including rusts are highly adapted to dispersal via the wind (Nagarajan and Singh 1990).
The development of disease epidemics in time and space is based on the dispersal of pathogen inoculum and repeated cycles of infection (Aylor 1990).
It is difficult to predict the movement, including direction, of airborne pathogens.
Normally, a large amount of spores of a pathogen will be deposited near the inoculum source (Roelfs and Martell 1984).
The migration and 11 distribution of stem rust “Ug99” from Uganda to other parts of Eastern Africa, Yemen and Iran is following predominant west-east airflows.
Plants may defend themselves against pathogens through passive protection mechanisms like the deposition of sticky or waxy substances around the locus of infection and performed anti-microbial compounds.
As a result, most plants are resistant to most plant pathogens (Dangle and Jones 2001).
Rust resistance genes in the host and dominant relationships of avirulence/virulence in the parasite are dependent on respective genotypes (Kolmer 1996).
Plant-pathogen interactions, particularly those involving biotrophic parasites, are governed by specific interactions between avirulence genes in the pathogen and the corresponding resistance gene locus in the host plant.
When corresponding resistance (R) and avirulence (Avr) genes are present in host and pathogen, respectively, the result is disease resistance.
To understand the genetic basis of resistance, understanding the terminologies is important.
Major genes are at risk due to pathogen plasticity (Singh and Rajaram 2002).
Non-specificity is only recognised by the absence of specificity and, because all tests are of limited size, the presence of race-non-specificity can never be proved (Johnson 1984).
It is not possible to define pathotypes based on this type of resistance, and it generally allows low level of rust sporulation (Parlevliet 1985; Singh and Rajaram 2002).
Slow rusting: is a type of resistance in which disease develops slowly, resulting in intermediate to low disease levels against all pathotypes of a pathogen (Caldwell 1968; Johnson 1984).
All these components can affect disease progress in the field (Singh and Rajaram 2002).
Susceptible wheat cultivars have larger and more uredinia than the slow rusting wheat cultivars.
Partial resistance: The definition of partial resistance is based on leaf rust resistance (caused by Puccinia hordei) in barley.
It is a form of incomplete resistance characterised by a reduced rate of disease spread despite a high or susceptible infection type (Parlevliet 1985).
Self-pollinating cereal crops like wheat are often grown over large areas as genetically uniform cultivars.
This gives the opportunity for the development and selection of new virulent pathotypes of a pathogen on particular cultivars.
While this may happen before the cultivar is widely exploited, certain cultivars have been grown widely for many years with the resistance present remaining effective (Johnson and Law 1975).
Quantitative resistance, usually under oligogenic or polygenic control, is generally more effective in the field and appears to be more durable.
Gene-for-gene hypothesis Flor studied the genetics of interaction between flax (Linum usitatissimum) and the flax rust pathogen Melampsora lini.
Based on these studies, he postulated specificity between single host resistance (R) genes and single pathogen avirulence (Avr) genes, known as the gene-for- gene hypothesis (Flor 1942, 1956).
However, a single host plant may contain many different R genes directed to a particular pathogen and a pathogen can have many Avr genes (Bent 1996).
Therefore, for a pathogen biotype to escape detection by a potential host, it must have recessive alleles for all of the relevant avirulence genes (Keen 1990).
The first race-specific avirulence gene cloned was isolated from race six of Pseudomonas syringae pv.
All linkage groups except Sr15/Lr20 involve transfers of genes (chromosome sections) between host species (Roelfs 1988b).

To identify any virulence changes in pathogens with respect to commercial cultivars being grown in specific areas.

Pathogenicity surveys in Australia have been conducted annually since 1919 (Park 2007).
Samples have also been received from farmers and breeders from different wheat growing regions of the country for analysis and identification.
Identification of pathogen and/or symptoms are universally known and accepted techniques in diagnosing the more common diseases (James 1974).
The methods used to measure disease vary according to the nature of the disease (Large 1966).
Accurate assessments of the losses caused by plant diseases are needed (Large 1966).
The measurement of cereal rust diseases can be qualitative, quantitative or a combination of both methods.
This helps in understanding the genetic nature of resistance, determining specific genes and mode of inheritance and interaction of resistance genes for breeding.
The approach uses different test cultivars with unknown genes for resistance along with control lines with known resistance genes.
To assess APR in a cultivar, the identity of seedling genes present and pathogenicity of pathogen pathotypes used for the test is essential.
Adult plants can be evaluated with the presence of seedling resistance genes in field nurseries by using pathotypes with virulence matching the seedling genes (Pathan and Park 2007).
Nonetheless, this analysis is time consuming because up to four generations may be required and tests of allelism may be needed (CIMMYT 1988).
The inheritance of resistance in various filial generations can be used to estimate the number of genes segregating for resistance in the cross.
F1 plants should be selfed and harvested individually to get F2 plants, or backcrossed to the susceptible parent to obtain B1CF1 plants.
The F2 or B1CF1 plants are then selfed and should be harvested individually to obtain F3 or B1CF2 families, respectively.
F3 and B1CF2 families can then be tested for resistance with different pathotypes of a pathogen and the segregating resistance genes will be used further in resistance gene identification.
There are shortcomings in using backcross ratios: in situations involving one dominant and one recessive resistance gene, the BC1 population segregation ratio will be same as for one dominant gene.
Moreover, the production of large backcross hybrid populations is laborious and costly.
The reaction of F3 generations to the disease can be used to confirm the F2 segregation ratio.
The isolation and characterisation of single genes in F3 families are more difficult when two or more genes are segregating, as many families will have more than one gene.
The other advantage using the backcross method is that the segregating genes can be evaluated in a background with 75% of the susceptible recurrent parent.
Unlike molecular markers, the expression of morphological and biochemical markers are influenced by environmental factors and plant growth stage (Winter and Kahl 1995).
Molecular markers are the most commonly used types of markers in plant breeding program due to their abundance.
The use of molecular markers is crucial in the analysis of genetic diversity and mapping of quantitative traits.
Quantitative trait loci (QTL) analysis offers a powerful tool for studying complex traits, including quantitative disease resistance (Young 1996).
Because of its complex and quantitative inheritance, understanding the basis of complex traits through genetic study and identification of QTL using conventional phenotypic trait values is difficult.
A QTL is a genomic region that controls variation in the quantitative trait of interest (Doerge 2002).
It can be a single gene or a cluster of linked genes that affect the trait.
Originally, genetic maps were prepared in tomato and maize by using molecular markers.
Molecular markers have many advantages as compared to the traditional phenotypic markers that were previously used.
Resistance genes have been characterised and tagged based on RFLPs and RAPDs molecular markers.
Pgt attacks not only wheat but also barley and some grasses, such as wild barley grass (Park 1997).
It is 22 also the most dangerous of the three rusts that affect wheat.
Stem rust is primarily a warm weather disease, but it can cause great damage to susceptible wheat crops over broad geographical regions.
In Australia, stem rust has threatened wheat since European settlement in the late 18th Century (McIntosh and Brown 1997).
Studies have reported significant losses from wheat stem rust in Australia (Park 2007).
The favorable environmental conditions and the presence of host plants year-round favour the survival and buildup of Pgt populations.
In 1998, a new pathotype of Pgt was detected on wheat in Uganda.
In temperate climates, teliospores, the resting spore stage, are produced near the end of the growing season of the host.
Each teliospore cell is dikaryotic when first formed, but karyogamy occurs with maturation of the teliospore (Leonard and Szabo 2005).
Pgt is characterised by the presence of uredinia, commonly on the leaf sheaths of the wheat plant, but also on true stem tissues, leaves, spikes, glumes, and awns.
On leaves, Pgt pustules develop mostly on the underside, but may penetrate and produce limited sporulation on the upper side.
Masses of urediniospores produced in the pustules are brownish red in color, and are easily dislodged from plants.
Wheat, barley, triticale, and a few related species are the primary hosts for Pgt.
The fungus represents a very broad spectrum of morphologic and biologic variability (Anikster and Wahl 1979).
The establishment of the disease on grasses increased its distribution worldwide (Anikster and Wahl 1979).
Long-distance dispersal is important for rust pathogens enabling their spores to colonise new regions rapidly (Brown and Hovmøller 2002).
Resistance genes Understanding the molecular and biochemical bases for resistance will lead to a better understanding of the genetic basis of resistance (Dubin and Brennan 2009).
Although genetic resistance against rust was used as early as in the 1880s, widely accepted resistant cultivars did not become available until the early 1940s (McIntosh and Brown 1997).
There are different levels of race-specific resistance to stem rust, which depend on the type of resistance gene/avirulence gene combination (Leonard and Szabo 2005).
Genetic resistance based upon a single R gene product in the host that recognises a single, complementary pathogen effector has been successful in protecting wheat from Pgt.
The wheat stem rust resistance genes Sr26, which was introgressed into wheat from Agropyron elongatum and Sr31, derived from rye can be considered durable.
The gene Sr26 was used widely in Australia from the 1970 onwards, yet rust pathotypes capable of overcoming it have not been detected (Park 2007).

Life cycle and host range Pst infects green tissues of cereal crops and grasses from early growth stages to maturity of the plant (Chen 2005).

The interaction between the environment, host and the pathogen itself dictate urediniospore germination.

Fungicides can be an important control option when rust epidemics are severe, however, their use results in significantly increased production costs for farmers (Hodson 2011).
In developed countries of Europe, Australia and the Americas, fungicides are at times used on a large scale as a key part of the national food security strategy (ICARDA 2011).
The use of fungicides in many parts of the world is however unaffordable.
Control strategies based on genetic resistance are considered the most cost-effective, environmentally safe and sustainable long- term option (Hodson 2011).
Genes conferring resistance against rust pathogens may be effective at all growth stages, or at post seedling and adult stages only.
The damage caused by leaf rust depends on the plant growth stage at the time of infection.
