Chi squared analysis (χ21R:1S = 0.82, P = 0.37) indicated monogenic inheritance (Lr26) when lines with ITs “X+3” or “3C” corresponding to Lr13 were placed in the susceptible category.
A range of resistant phenotypes was observed among the 126 DH lines in the field.
However, leaf rust infection was distributed more in to resistant category than susceptible.
The QTLs located on chromosome 3AS and 4D were contributed by Rialto, whereas the 3BS QTL was contributed by the parent Spark.
The SSR marker barc12 was closely linked with QLr.sun-3AS and explained 11–19% phenotypic variation.
In view of this genetic association, this QTL was considered for further fine mapping.
Likewise, Rialto allele at the psp3103 locus showed 4.7–8.78% lower leaf rust response compared with Spark allele at the same locus.
On the other hand, a 13.02–20.11% lower disease response was recorded at the cfb5006 locus contributed by Spark allele than the Rialto allele at the same marker locus (Table 3.5).
There were 11 DH lines with all three QTL combinations and showed a mean leaf rust disease severity of 1.24%.
Four lines carrying only QLr.sun-3AS showed lower mean disease severity (7.09%) when compared to the mean disease serveries of QTL QLr.sun-3BS (13.6%) or QLr.sun-4D (18.02%) when present alone.
Conversely, eight DH lines that carried 47 QLr.sun-4D alone showed higher mean disease severity (18.02%) than QLr.sun-3AS and QLr.sun-3BS when present alone or in combination.
Overall, highly resistant DH lines resulted when all three QTLs were present together.
Fine mapping of QLr.sun-3BS QLr.sun-3BS was fine mapped by enriching the encompassed region with SSR, DArT, STS and SNP markers.
Initially, 40 SSR, DArT and STS markers located on this chromosome were screened to determine polymorphism between the two parents and the bulks.
Of these 40 markers, eight were polymorphic and were genotyped on the whole DH population.
The linkage map was reconstructed by adding the new markers and composite interval mapping was conducted using WinQTL cartographer.
After saturation of chromosome 3BS with SSR and SNP markers, QLr.sun-3BS explained field phenotypic variance ranging from 18–22% (Table 3.6).
When genotyped with SSR, DArT and SNP markers spanning the QLr.sun-3BS region, the segregation ratio of each marker within the population fitted a 1:2:1 ratio.
All 382 F2 individuals derived from these three crosses were also susceptible when inoculated with the same pathotype used to test F1 plants (Table 3.8).
Among the 21 Australian wheat cultivars, four (EGA Bonnie Rock, Giles, Hyperno, and Wyalkatchen) were positive for both markers.
Susceptible lines included as a negative control in both European winter wheats and Australian genotypes produced amplification products as expected.
However, it can provide good level of protection when present in combination with other resistance genes (Kolmer 1992a).
For example, Lr13 in combination with Lr34 has been related to durable resistance (Roelfs 1988a).
The combination of Lr13 with the seedling resistance gene Lr16 can also enhance resistance (Samborski and Dyck 1982; Dadkhodaie 2008).
In addition to seedling resistance genes Lr13 and Lr26, this study also identified three consistent and significant QTLs conferring APR to leaf rust over the three years.
Of the three QTLs, two (QLr.sun-3AS and QLr.sun-4D) were contributed by Rialto and one (QLr.sun- 3BS) was contributed by parent Spark.
Leaf rust severity was compared for the three years by identifying DH lines that carried these QTLs alone and in combination.
The mean disease severities of lines without the QTLs were significantly higher than lines with either of the QTLs or in combination.
This may needs further work to confirm, if the two loci are closely linked or not.
The 3BS leaf rust QTL is a new APR locus and SSR markers gwm533 and gwm493 initially flanked this locus.
The APR on 3BS was temporarily designated LrSpa and fine mapped by enriching the encompassed region of QLr.sun-3BS.
Once reliable markers linked closely to the target trait or QTL are located, they can be then used confidently for MAS breeding (Collard and Mackill 2008).
QTL QLr.sun-3BS was Mendelised using an F3 population derived from a cross between a line carrying LrSpa only and a leaf rust 57 susceptible genotype.
Results of tests of allelism between LrSpa and Lr12 strongly suggested that LrSpa and Lr27 are different.
Similarly, Hartog amplified the fragment band of 337 bp when tested with the other Sr2 linked CAPS marker csSr2, while the parents and the bulks were null.
Sr2 is also known to be associated with a trait known as pseudo-black chaff (PBC), which causes pigmentation of stems and/or glumes (McFadden 1939; Hare and McIntosh 1979).
This coincides with the same region and interval in which LrSpa was mapped in the present study.
This may suggest that LrSV2 and LrSpa could be allelic or linked.
Allelism tests have been initiated to resolve the relationship between LrSpa and LrSV2.
The closely linked SNP markers BS00004074 and BS00010945 linked to LrSpa identified in our study can facilitate marker-assisted selection of this gene in breeding.
Both markers were equally good and produced similar results in our studies, and we assume that both could be used reliably for MAS.
As no other adult plant leaf rust resistance gene is located in chromosome 3BS, we propose that the LrSpa be formally named and have submitted a case for gene designation.
Stem rust, caused by Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici (Pgt), is historically among the most important and devastating diseases of wheat on a global basis.
In susceptible cultivars, yield loss due to stem rust can be as high as 100% (Singh and Rajaram 2002).
The narrow genetic basis of resistance to stem rust in countries like Ethiopia has also contributed to the vulnerability of the available genetic resources to the pathogen population.
More recently, another stem rust outbreak has occurred in Ethiopia, which caused yield losses up to 100% in severely affected areas.
Genetic resistance is considered the most effective and sustainable way of controlling this disease, particularly for farmers in developing countries where use of fungicides is unaffordable.
The use of adult plant resistance (APR) genes associated with slow rusting minor genes is believed to offer more durable resistance to the rust diseases of wheat.
The slow rusting, durable gene Lr34/Yr18 that provides partial leaf rust and stripe rust resistance has also been effective since the early 20th Century (Singh 1992).
The development of molecular markers that are closely linked to target traits is important in expediting reliable selection and pyramiding of different genes in wheat breeding.
Genetic mapping has been used effectively in identifying regions in the wheat genome that confer resistance to Pgt (Haile and Röder 2013).
A total of 126 DH lines were used for greenhouse and field stem rust phenotyping and QTL mapping.
Eight to 10 seedlings per line were evaluated in 9 cm plastic pots.
The pots were fertilised with complete fertiliser, Aquasol®, at the rate of 25 g/101 water for 200 pots.
Six to seven-day old seedlings were again treated with a nitrogenous fertiliser, Nitram® (25 g/101 of water for 200 pots).
Pots were moved to microclimate rooms maintained at 15–20°C until they were ready for inoculation.
To avoid contamination, the spray equipment was washed in alcohol and rinsed in running tap water between successive inoculations.
Inoculated plants were incubated and placed in water- filled steel trays covered with polythene hoods that maintained 100% relative humidity within 63 a greenhouse room.
Inoculated seedlings were incubated for 48 hours at a temperature maintained between 20‒25°C.
The incubated seedlings were then transferred to a temperature and irrigation controlled greenhouse growth rooms at 24‒26°C until ready for disease assessment.
The symbols ‘C’ and ‘N’ were used to indicate chlorosis and necrosis, respectively, associated with the ITs.
Plus and minus signs were used to denote larger or smaller than normal uredinia respectively within a given IT.
Genetic heterogeneity was represented by listing ITs on individual plants separated by comma, with the most frequent IT written first.
When two types of ITs were observed on a single leaf, they were listed together without comma (e.g. “2+3”).
ITs “X” (mesothetic reaction, random distribution of variable sized uredinia, or when both resistant and susceptible ITs observed in the same leaf) was regarded as resistant.
Approximately 20–30 seeds were planted evenly in a 0.75 m row with a spreader strip comprising stem rust susceptible genotypes adjacent to each row.
The two parental lines were included at the beginning, middle and end of each nursery as controls.
Disease scoring began when the spreader rows displayed a highly susceptible reaction.
QTLs were considered significant at P < 0.05, with logarithm of odds (LOD) score determined by 1,000 tests for each trait (Doerge and Churchill 1996).
Linkage groups were assigned to chromosomes on the basis of previously mapped and known genomic positions of the markers.
A total of 281 markers were used to localise the QTLs in the mapping population.
The infection types were similar to those produced by the Sr31 control genotype Mildress (Table 4.2).
However, with pathotype 21-0 (avirulent to both Sr5 and Sr31), Rialto produced IT “0;”, typical to that produced by the differential genotype carrying Sr5.
On this basis, the seedling genes Sr5 and Sr31 were postulated in Rialto.
The genotypes that showed IT “0;” were postulated to carry either Sr5 or Sr5 +Sr31, whereas those showing ITs “2-” to “2-C” were postulated to carry only Sr31.
Frequency distribution of the adult plant stem rust infection observed across the DH lines was bimodally distributed in all four experiments (Figures 4.2 and 4.3).
The population showed the same pattern of segregation across all four experiments, and Chi- squared analysis supported the involvement of three genes (segregation ratio 7:1, Table 4.4).
The reistance gene Lr26/Sr31/Yr9 could not be precisely located on the 70 chromosome arm 1R1B using this population.
Composite interval mapping (CIM) of field data with 281 markers using QTL Cartographer revealed involvement of resistance loci on chromosomes 1BS, 3BS and 5A across all data sets.
The QTL detected on chromosome 1BS, temporarily designated QSr.sun-1BS, was associated with the marker gwm18, where the major seedling resistance gene Sr31 was also located and contributed by Rialto.
The QTL located on chromosome 3BS, designated QSr.sun-3BS was closely associated with SSR marker gwm1034 and the QTL detected on 5A (QSr.sun-5A) was closely linked with SSR marker gwm443.
The QTL QSr.sun-1BS (Sr31) was significantly associated with stem rust resistance and explained 73–84% of the phenotypic variation for this trait.
The phenotypic variation explained by the QTL QSr.sun-3BS was between 6% and 12%.
Lines carrying Spark allele at gwm443 locus showed a reduction in stem rust severity of 13.09-16.85% when compared with lines that carried Rialto allele at the same locus (Table 4.7).
In addition to these consistent QTLs, other minor QTLs were also detected by the CIM analysis.
The mean stem rust severity of 20 lines (54.1%) with no QTL was higher than lines with any QTL, whether present singly or in combination.
However, as Lr26 is completely linked with Sr31 and Yr9, it is very unlikely that the additional six lines carry Lr26 without Sr31.
The most probable reason for this discrepancy is misclassification of the lines.
The low infection type is usually very low (“0” to “;”) but it gives relatively higher infection types when it is transferred to susceptible genetic background (Luig and Rajaram 1972).
Genetic linkage map based on the Pgt pathotype 21-0 located the gene Sr5 on chromosome 6DS associated with DArT marker wPt-3879 (data not shown).
The resistance gene Sr31 is known to be located in the 1BL/1RS translocation and has contributed significantly to global wheat production.
Thus, this gene is effectively used in many wheat-growing countries free of “Ug99”.
However, Sr31 has not been widely used in Australia due to its association with poor bread making quality (McIntosh 1988).
Sr2 was mapped on chromosome 3BS and is associated with the dark pigmentation trait pseudo black chaff (PBC) (Hare and McIntosh 1979).
In this study, PBC was not detected in either the parents or any of the DH lines, indicating the APR in the population is unlikely controlled by Sr2.
In the current study, three consistent APR QTLs were detected on chromosomes 1BS, 3BS and 5A, which contributed field resistance and reduced stem rust severity significantly.
While this QTL displayed the largest phenotypic variation, it had the most significant effect in reducing stem rust severity in the field.
Through monosomic analysis, Sr14 was mapped on the long arm of chromosome 1B (McIntosh 1980).
Thus, further testing and mapping of the common markers could help to clearly understand and determine whether the QTL QSr.sun-1BS and Sr31 are same or not.
The second consistent QTL, QSr.sun-3BS, was located on chromosome 3BS on which it mapped closely to the SSR marker gwm1034.
However, in all of these studies the authors 78 stated that the QTL identified could be Sr2.
The third consistent QTL detected on chromosome 5A for APR to stem rust resistance was minor and contributed by the moderately susceptible parent Spark.
Further work is therefore required to resolve the relationships between these loci.
Three additional inconsistent minor QTLs were detected on chromosomes 3A and 4BL from Rialto and 6A from Spark.
These QTLs might contribute significantly to reducing stem rust severity when present in combination with the other QTLs.
Hence, further testing of the population for additional years/sites or application of more markers may be needed to determine the effectiveness of these QTLs.
Stripe rust, caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici (Pst), is one of the most destructive and widespread diseases of wheat on a global basis.
Regular rust epidemics have occurred that have resulted in significant yield losses and low grain quality (Line and Chen 1995).
Stripe rust can cause yield losses of 10‒70% depending on cultivar response, earliness of initial infection, rate of disease development and the duration of infection (Chen 2005).
It caused significant yield losses throughout the eastern wheat belt in the mid-1980s (Wellings 2007).
Since the detection of the first pathotype 104 E137 A- in Victoria, many pathotypes emerged increasingly through mutation and have challenged Australian wheat production (Park 2008).
Because of this pathotype, crop damage 80 was widespread and high in different wheat growing regions of the country from 2002 to 2005.
Derivative pathotypes with virulence for Yr17, Yr27, Yr10, and two genes in triticale (YrJ and YrT) have since been detected (Wellings 2007).
The use of genetic resistance is the most economical and environmentally safe method of controlling stripe rust.
Adult plant resistance (APR) genes associated with slow rusting are believed to be more durable for successful long-term rust control in wheat.
The slow rusting, durable resistance gene Yr18/Lr34 that provides partial stripe rust and leaf rust resistance has been effective since the early 20th Century (Singh 1992).
The development of molecular markers that are closely linked to target traits is important in allowing reliable selection and pyramiding of different genes in wheat breeding.
Breeding for rust resistance is an ongoing process and development of cultivars with durable resistance relies on characterisation and increasing the genetic diversity of resistance sources, especially APR.
The present study was carried out to determine the genetic basis of the resistance in both cultivars, and to characterise the genes responsible.
A total of 126 DH lines were used for greenhouse and field stripe rust phenotyping.
Eight to 10 seedlings per line were evaluated in 9 cm diameter plastic pots.
The pots were supplemented with a balanced fertiliser, Aquasol®, at the rate of 25 g/101 water for 200 pots.
After fertiliser application, seeds were sown and covered with potting mix (80% composted pine and 20% coarse sand).
Inoculated plants were incubated and placed in water- filled steel trays covered with polythene hoods that maintained 100% relative humidity with in a greenhouse room.
Inoculated plants were incubated at 11°C for 18–24 hours in a dark room.
The incubated seedlings were then moved to a temperature and irrigation controlled greenhouse growth rooms at 17–18°C until ready for disease assessment.
Plus and minus signs were used to denote larger or smaller than normal uredinia, respectively within a given IT.
When two types of ITs were observed on a single leaf, they were listed together without comma (e.g. “1+2”).
Approximately 20–30 seeds were planted in a 0.75 m row with a spreader strip with stripe rust susceptible cultivars adjacent to each row.
The time of sowing varied between years from the end of April through the beginning of May.
Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici pathotypes used in greenhouse and field tests Pst pathotype Culture no.
The F3 lines were scored as non-segregating 84 resistant (NSR), segregating (SEG) and non-segregating susceptible (NSS) to Pst.
A total of 281 markers were used to establish marker-trait associations in the mapping population.
In the field, epidemic development of stripe rust progressed well in all years with the spreader rows developing 100% infection.
Both parental lines displayed very high levels of resistance across all experiments (Table 5.2).
The segregation patterns and number of resistance genes observed varied with the different pathotypes.
When the DH population was tested with pathotype 238 E143 A+, one-gene segregation ratio was observed (Table 5.3).
The resistance was contributed by Spark as seedlings of Rialto showed high IT with this pathotype.
To identify the chromosomal location of the gene, preliminary mapping of the DH lines was conducted using 281 markers.
All the lines showed a high level of resistance (CI value of “0” to “0.1”) to the pathotypes used in the field.
No lines were observed to be susceptible against field Pst pathotypes across all data sets, in which both the parents displayed high levels of resistance.
This suggested that the two cultivars shared one or more genes conferring resistance allele to stripe rust.
All the three populations showed a satisfactory fit to a 7:8:1 ratio, suggesting that two genes were involved in controlling stripe rust resistance in the field.
The same SpRi74/Avocet, SpRi37/Avocet and SpRi87/Avocet populations were phenotyped in the greenhouse using one of the pathotypes used in the field, 134 E16 A+ YrJ+ YrT+.
The parents SpRi37, SpRi74 and SpRi87 showed infection types of “;N”, indicating a presence of seedling resistance gene(s) effective against pt. 134 E16 A+ YrJ+ YrT+ in all.
The distribution of resistance in all the three F3 populations revealed 1:2:1 segregation ratio, indicating the presence of single seedling resistance gene (Table 5.4).
However, the F3’s segregated for a single gene against pathotype 134 E16 A+ YrJ+ YrT+, which is virulent to Yr6 and Yr7 and avirulent to Yr3 and Yr4.
Based on the Yr4 linked SSR marker barc75, the only parent considered to carry Yr4 was SpRi74.
Thus, the single gene present in SpRi37 and SpRi87 was considered likely to be Yr3, and in SpRi74 Yr4, both of which were also effective in the field.
The discrepancies between these results may be attributed to different seed sources.
Application of the SSR marker barc75 on the DH population further supported the likely presence of Yr4 in the population, detected in 41 lines.
The marker amplified a positive product in parent Rialto and a band different from the Yr4 positive control Rubric was amplified in Spark.
As cultivar Moulin is present in the pedigrees of both Rialto and Spark, Yr3 and Yr4 may have been derived from this cultivar.
Yr6 is frequent in both spring wheat and winter wheat and is also present in the pedigrees of Spark and Rialto.
Many stripe rust resistance genes have been reported previously on chromosome 2B.
These studies indicate that YrSpa is distinct from Yr5 or Yr7 based on its mapping on short arm of 2B in comparison to long arm location of Yr5 and Yr7.
Further YrSpa and Yr7 could be differentiated based on response to pathotype 238 E143 A+, Yr7 being ineffective and YrSpa effective to this pathotype.
The leaf rust resistance gene Lr13 was identified in both parents Spark and Rialto in another study (Chapter 3).
The IT displayed by YrSpa (“2+”) was distinct from Yr27 and without black necrosis.
Additionally, YrSpa was resistant against pathotype 134 E16 A+ Yr17+ Yr27+, while Yr27 was ineffective, indicating the two genes are not identical.
The markers detected in this study are loosely linked to the gene YrSpa, therefore YrSpa could either be same gene as Yr31, Yr41, YrSP or new.
Hence, further refinement of the map and identifying closely linked markers is necessary to resolve this issue and describe the gene.
Under field conditions, the parents and all DH lines were found to be highly resistant (ITs of “0” to “TR”) against the field pathotypes across all data sets.
The complete absence of segregation in the population for susceptibility suggested that the parents likely share one or more common resistance allele(s).
Because the field pathotypes were avirulent for the uncharacterised seedling gene, it was not possible to chacracterise APR in the DH population.
Putative single gene APR lines (lacking seedling resistance) were identified and further studies are needed to resolve the identity of adult plant resistance.
It is the fourth most important cereal crop in the country next to Teff, Maize and Sorghum in area sown, and third in total productivity (CSA 2009).
Of the total area under wheat, durum wheat covers 60% and common wheat the remaining 40% (Gebre-Mariam 1991; Pecetti and Damania 1996).
The great genetic variability of tetraploid wheat makes Ethiopia a center of outstanding genetic diversity (Vavilov 1929).
However, problems associated with both biotic and abiotic stresses often affect wheat production in the country significantly.
Leaf rust is the most regularly occurring and widely distributed of the three rust diseases.
The damage caused by leaf rust is usually less than by stem rust and stripe rust, but depends on plant growth stage at the time of infection.
If infection occurs early, it can cause extensive yield losses; 60–70%, infection on the flag leaf at spike emergence may cause grain yield losses of more than 30%.
Historically, stem rust has been the major threat to world wheat production (Saari and Prescott 1985).
Because of the widespread use of resistant cultivars, the disease was managed successfully for over three decades.
In 2013, a stem rust epidemic occurred in the districts of Agarfa and Gasera in Bale zone Region on cultivar Digalu.
This shows that rust pathogens are ongoing threats to wheat production worldwide.
It is believed to have caused recurrent, severe losses in crops since the dawn of agriculture (ICARDA 2011).
It caused 40% yield losses in those countries and destroyed 80% of the wheat crop in some areas of Ethiopia (ICARDA 2012).
The disease is prevalent mostly in the highlands of Ethiopia, where common wheat is largely grown.
The use of genetic resistance is the most common, economic and environmentally friendly way of managing rust diseases.
Sets of Australian leaf rust, stem rust and stripe rust differentials with known resistance genes and susceptible controls were also used.
The genotypes were screened against specific pathotypes of Pt, Pgt and Pst at the seedling stage in the greenhouse and at adult plant growth stages in 97 field.
A total of eight to 10 seedlings were grown per genotype in 9 cm plastic pots in each experiment.
Complete nitrogenous fertiliser, Aquasol®, at the rate of 25 g/101 water for 200 pots, was used to fertilise the pots.
Seedlings were raised in microclimate rooms maintained at 15–20°C until they were ready for inoculation.
Plants were again treated with a nitrogenous fertiliser, Nitram® (25 g/101 of water for 200 pots) after seven days.
The spray equipment was washed in 70% alcohol and rinsed in running tap water to avoid contamination between successive inoculations.
For leaf rust, inoculated plants were placed in a dew chamber for 24 hours at ambient temperature in a dark room, in which mist was generated by an ultrasonic humidifier.
For stem rust and stripe rust, inoculated seedlings were placed in water-filled steel trays covered with polythene hoods that maintained 100% relative humidity.
Leaf rust infection types (ITs) were scored 10–12 days after inoculation, stem rust 14 days after inoculation and stripe rust 17 days after inoculation.
In this scale, ITs lower than “3” were considered as incompatible (resistant reaction) and regarded as low infection type (LIT).
ITs “3” or greater were considered as compatible (susceptible response) and regarded as high infection type (HIT).
For leaf rust and stem rust, ITs “X” (mesothetic reaction, when both resistant and susceptible ITs were observed in the same leaf) and considered as resistant.
Approximately 20–30 seeds of each test genotype were sown in 0.75 m rows.
After every five rows of test genotypes, a row comprising a mixture of susceptible cultivars was sown as a rust spreader.
The disease score began when the spreader rows displayed a highly susceptible reaction.
Host reaction types were scored following the scale given in Table 6.3.
Debre-Zeit and Njoro are internationally selected “hot spots” for screening nurseries for stem rust.
All 78 common and non-common wheat genotypes were characterised with four markers, SNP1G22, csGs, csSr2, and barc75, specific to Lr46, Lr68, Sr2 and Yr4, respectively.
The genotypes Baxter, LB +Lr46, RL6077, Parula, Diamondbird and Rubric were used as positive controls for Lr34, Lr46, Lr67, Lr68, Sr2 and Yr4, respectively, for marker screening.
Leaves from 8–10 plants of each genotype were collected in 2 ml Eppendorf tubes 9–12 days after sowing.
To dry the leaf tissue, the tubes were kept for 3–4 days on silica beads.
Chloroform: phenol (700 µl, 24:1 v/v) was added and the tubes were shaken to mix the contents properly.
Samples were centrifuged for 20 min at 4,000 and 650 µl of the supernatant was transferred to new tubes.
The contents were mixed thoroughly and kept in a freezer (-20°C) for 20 min.
To precipitate the DNA, the tubes were again centrifuged for 10 min at 10, 000 rpm.
To dissolve the DNA pellet, tubes were then kept for 2–3 hrs in an oven (37°C).
DNA samples were then quantified using a Nanodrop ND- 1000 spectrophotometer (Nanodrop Technologies).
A 30 ng/µl DNA dilution of all samples was prepared with double distilled and autoclaved water (ddH2O) for use in PCR.
PCR products were separated on 2.5% agarose gel and visualised under UV light.
SNP genotyping of Lr46 and Lr67 linked markers was carried out as mentioned in chapter three.

Landraces of crop species have yet to be employed in plant breeding because they are most genetically diverse both between and within populations (Brown and Munday 1982).
Therefore, evaluation of Ethiopian landraces especially durum and emmer wheats would greatly be useful for resistance breeding against rust pathogens.
In conclusion, in the current study, most of the genotypes were shown to carry uncharacterised seedling and adult plant resistance gene(s) especially to stem rust and stripe rust.
These resistances could be potentially very useful in developing new cultivars with adequate and durable resistance to the rust pathogens.
Although rust diseases can be controlled by fungicide applications, the use of resistant cultivars is considered the most economically affordable, efficient and ecologically friendly control method.
Gene postulation helps to quickly identify the absence of race- specific seedling resistance genes and those that might be present (Kolmer 2003).
Being polygenic in nature, breeding for durable resistance based on minor genes is difficult and time consuming through conventional breeding methods.
This requires ongoing research efforts in identifying new and potentially durable sources of genetic resistance.
Continuous efforts in identification and characterisation of diverse sources of resistance are crucial to develop new resistant cultivars.
A DH mapping population derived from the cross between Spark and Rialto was evaluated in the greenhouse and field for reaction to leaf rust.
Based on seedling tests with four Puccinia triticina (Pt) pathotypes, two major seedling leaf rust resistance genes (Lr13 in both Spark and Rialto; and Lr26 in Rialto) were identified.
Simultaneous stem rust and stripe rust tests postulated the linked genes Sr31 and Yr9 in the DH population.
QTL mapping of APR data revealed three consistent resistance loci for leaf rust on chromosomes 3AS (QLr.sun-3AS), 3BS (QLr.sun-3BS) and 4D (QLr.sun-4D).
QTLs QLr.sun-3AS and QLr.sun-4D were inherited from Rialto, while QLr.sun-3BS from Spark.
DH lines that carried these QTLs in combination exhibited lower leaf rust responses than lines with either of the QTLs, showed the additive nature of the QTLs.
QTLs QLr.sun-3AS and QLr.sun-3BS had a larger and significant effect on lowering leaf rust severity, while QLr.sun-4D was very minor.
Initially, the 3BS QTL was thought to be associated with a QTL for stem rust resistance and was considered for further fine mapping.
However, further studies revealed that there was no association between leaf rust and stem rust phenotypic data and the two loci are independent.
This may need further work to confirm, if the two loci are closely linked or not.
Of these, four SSR and five SNP markers showed linkage with the QTL QLr.sun-3BS.
Based on the presence/absence of these markers, LrSpa was common in these germplasm.
LrSpa is likely to be a new locus as no other gene conferring APR to Pt has been reported on chromosome 3BS.
To determine the genetic relationship between LrSpa and Lr27, allelism tests were conducted.
F1 and F2 populations were derived from crossing lines carrying LrSpa (but lacking Lr26) with lines carrying Lr12 (Tc +Lr12).
Because Lr12 is linked to or same gene as Lr31, the F1 derived from cross of Lr27/LrSpa and Lr12/Lr31 must be resistant because of complementary expression of Lr27 +Lr31.
Pseudo-black chaff (PBC), which is associated with Sr2 (McFadden 1939; Hare and McIntosh 1979) was not observed in the DH population, providing further evidence that Lr27 is absent in Spark.
LrSpa as well as the associated markers BS00004074 and BS00010945 identified in this study will enhance and facilitate marker assisted selection and the potential for achieving durable resistance.
The DH lines were also evaluated for their response to stem rust both at seedling stage in the greenhouse and at adult plant stage in the field.
Phenotyping in the greenhouse with three Pgt pathotypes identified two seedling resistance genes, Sr5 and Sr31 in Rialto.
As there is no pathotype virulent on Sr31 in Australia, all the DH lines that carry Sr31 were highly resistant in the field.
In field tests, parent Spark was moderately susceptible, while Rialto was highly resistant.
Marker analysis of adult plant data detected three consistent APR QTLs on chromosome 1BS (QSr.sun-1BS), 3BS (QSr.sun-3BS) and 5A (QSr.sun-5A) that contributed field resistance and reduced stem rust severity significantly.
Of these, QSr.sun-1BS was contributed by Rialto, whereas the remaining two were contributed by Spark.
The SSR marker gwm18 was identified as the closest marker to the gene.
Further studies are required with additional markers for genotyping the population to clearly understand and determine whether QSr.sun-1BS and Sr31 are same, linked or allelic.
QSr.sun-3BS and QSr.sun-5A were minor QTLs and mapped very close to the SSR markers gwm1034 and gwm443, respectively.
These markers could be very useful in further refining the maps and to develop diagnostic markers for marker-assisted breeding.
Additionally, three inconsistent minor QTLs were also detected on chromosome 3A (QSr.sun-3A), 4BL (QSr.sun-4BL), contributed by Rialto and 6A (QSr.sun-6A) contributed by Spark.
The QTLs QSr.sun-3A, QSr.sun-4BL and QSr.sun-6A were all detected in three of the four data sets only.
Therefore, further studies are needed to characterise, fine map and confirm these QTLs.
Overall, the QTLs identified in this study will be useful as additional resistance sources for enhancing characterisation of APR to stem rust in breeding programs.
Through multipathotype testing, resistance genes Yr3, Yr4, Yr6, Yr7 and Yr9 and one uncharacterised seedling resistance (USR) were postulated.
Preliminary genetic mapping was conducted on the basis of seedling data with pathotype 238 E16 A+, in which the USR gene was mapped on chromosome 2BS.
However, both markers reported in the current study are loosely linked to YrSpa and unable to distinguish whether this gene is the same as Yr31, Yr41, YrSP or new.
Therefore, refining of this locus and identifying closely linked markers will be worth pursuing in further studies.
No segregation for susceptibility was observed, indicating that the two parents probably share common resistance allele(s).
When the F3 populations were evaluated under field conditions, the segregation ratios indicated the presence of two genes controlling the resistance.
The segregation pattern fitted well with a single gene model when tested with pathotype 134 E16 A+ YrJ+ YrT+ in the greenhouse, which was used in the field.
A high level of resistance observed in the DH population under field conditions needs further investigation and could be very useful in resistance breeding to stripe rust.
TTKSK was considered as a major threat to food security as the pathotype and its derivatives are virulent on most of the major resistance genes.
Stripe rust epidemics were also recorded in different years in Ethiopia with severe loss in 1988 in common wheat (Badebo and Bayu 1991).
Therefore, identification and characterisation of genetically diverse sources of resistance is critical.
On the basis of multipathotype tests with 10 Pt pathotypes, 42 genotypes lacked any detectable seedling resistance.
Five seedling resistance genes Lr1, Lr13, Lr16, Lr23 and Lr73 either singly or in combination were postulated in 14 genotypes.
In field tests, 50 genotypes displayed highly to moderately resistant responses to leaf rust against the Pt pathotypes used.
On the other hand, 19 genotypes displayed high level of leaf rust against the Pt pathotypes in the field.
Considering this, the genotypes were screened with Lr34, Lr46, Lr67 and Lr68 linked markers csLV34, SNP1G22, TM4KASPar and csGs, respectively.
Of the 20 common wheat genotypes tested with Lr34 and Lr67 linked markers, only two were found to be postulated to carry Lr67.
Of the 78 genotypes tested with markers SNP1G22, csGs for the presence of Lr46 and Lr68, respectively, 41 genotypes were postulated to have Lr46 and seven Lr68.
Variable levels of leaf rust severity (highly resistant to susceptible) were observed with genotypes carrying these APR genes.
The genotype Abyssinia 23 (AUS4045) lacked detectable seedling resistance but carried the APR genes Lr46 and Lr67.
Therefore, high level of field resistance in this genotype could be due to the presence of additional APR gene(s) in combination with Lr46 and Lr67.
In studies of stem rust, all the genotypes were screened in the greenhouse against nine Pgt pathotypes.
Resistance genes Sr8a, Sr8b, Sr9b, Sr9e and Sr13 were postulated to be present in nine genotypes.
Sr9e occurred with the highest frequency (in five genotypes), and the remaining genes each were postulated in a single genotype.
The identity of seedling resistance gene(s) in 59 genotypes could not be determined with the array of Pgt pathotypes used.
In the field, most of the genotypes displayed highly resistant (61.54%) to moderately resistant (24.36%) responses.
Among these, seven genotypes lacked detectable seedling resistance, eight genotypes were postulated to carry designated seedling genes and the remaining 52 genotypes were predicted to have uncharacterised seedling resistance gene(s).
In order to identify new sources of stem rust resistance against “Ug99”, 44 durum and 34 non- common wheat genotypes were evaluated in Ethiopia and Kenya, respectively.
Similarly, the genotypes tested in Kenya showed stem rust response scores varying from “1” to “6” against the “Ug99” pathotype TTKST and other Pgt pathotypes used in 2013.
Therefore, these genotypes can be very useful to facilitate breeding for resistance against “Ug99”.
Marker genotyping using the Sr2 linked marker csSr2 indicated the presence of Sr2 in only three genotypes (Abyssinia 24 (AUS4048), Abyssinia 25 and J H Parker 53).
The genotypes were highly resistant to moderately resistant against Pgt in field evaluations.
All the genotypes were screened at seedling stage in the greenhouse with 12 Pst pathotypes for stripe rust resistance.
Resistance genes Yr4, Yr6, Yr7 and Yr24 were postulated in five genotypes.
Fifty-five genotypes were postulated to carry uncharacterised gene(s), because the ITs did not match with any of the differential genotypes with known genes.
Three genotypes displayed moderate levels of resistance and the remaining 66 genotypes were highly resistant to Pst.
As mentioned earlier, genotypes were genotyped using markers csLV34, SNP1G22, TM4KASPar and barc75, which are linked to resistance genes Lr34, Lr46, Lr67 and Yr4, respectively.
Based on the results, Yr29/Lr46 postulated in 41 and Yr46/Lr67 in two genotypes, whereas Yr18/Lr34 was not detected in any of the common wheat genotypes tested.
Similarly, all the genotypes were tested with Yr4 linked barc75, from which only nine genotypes amplified the marker allele.
Overall, most Ethiopian genotypes evaluated in the current study were shown to carry uncharacterised seedling resistance and were resistant under field conditions especially to Pgt and Pst pathotypes.
Characterisation and evaluation of Ethiopian landraces, especially durum and emmer wheats, would 190 therefore greatly enhance the potential to find resistance sources for breeding against rust pathogens.
In the study conducted, a new slow rusting APR gene from Spark, LrSpa, to Pt was characterised and mapped on chromosome 3BS.
Additional novel QTLs associated with leaf rust and stem rust were detected and mapped in different chromosomes in the DH population.
Fine mapping of the QTL regions is required in order to identify the APR genes involved.
Genetic studies on three F3 populations indicated the involvement of an APR gene in addition to either Yr3, Yr4 or YrSpa.
Through multipathotype tests, field tests and application of gene specific molecular markers, majority of the Ethiopian genotypes were found to carry uncharacterised seedling and APR genes to the three rusts.
Therefore, further work is necessary to fully characterise and assess the resistance genes present in the genotypes.

The pathogens are obligate parasites that co-evolved with their hosts in a system greatly influenced by the environment.
This review presents a historical retrospective of cereal rusts as well as aspects of their biology, such as taxonomy, life cycle, physiological specialization and the process of infection.
In addition, more specific details are presented for each of the main rusts of wheat, barley, oats and rye.
Methods of controlling them, particularly genetic, chemical and through cultural practices are also presented.
THE CEREAL RUSTS IN HISTORY Rusts are known as the most destructive of the cereal dis- eases and since Ancient times have had a great influence on human civilizations.
The first knowledge of famine that can be attributed to rust is in the Old Testament, in the story of Joseph in Egypt, 1,800 BC.
A scienti- fic evidence of this occurrence in Ancient times was provi- ded by excavations in Israel.
Every Spring, on April 25th, a ceremony which in- volved sacrificing reddish colored animals, such dogs or cows to appease Robigus and induce him to hold back his vengeances.
This weather was undoubtedly respon- sible for heavy losses due to wheat rusts.
With these losses came hunger, discontent, famine and diseases, as typhus, plague and other decimating scourges of mankind, which helped to destroy the Roman civilization.
By this time men turned away from natural history and its branches for 1000 years, until the 15th century, with the re- birth of learning.
Later, in 1797, Persoon named the causal organism as Puc- cinia graminis, although in the first registered documents, a distinction between leaf and stem rusts was not made (Chester 1946).
As early as 1805, Prevost in France, and Sir J. Banks in England, suspected that red and black rusts were somehow closely connected.
More than a half century elapsed before the Tulasne brothers confirmed this suspicion and proved that indeed they were really two phases of the same disease (Carefoot and Sprott 1967).
Plant pathologists found out long before the 20th century that understanding the life history is not enough, but the host plant must be studied in all its pha- ses, too.
The five spore stages can differ from each other in ap- pearance, ploidy, pathogenicity, virulence, structures formed, and mechanism of penetration (Heath 1997; Staples 2000).
Each teliospore cell is dikaryotic when first formed, but kariogamy occurs early in teliospore maturation.
Teliospores remain dormant in the infected straw until spring, when they germinate in synchrony with the new leaf growth in the alternate, non-gramineous host.
With spring rains and favorable temperatures, one or both cells of the teliospores germinates, undergoes meiosis and produces a four-celled hyphal protrusion called a promyce- lium or basidium.
When meiosis is completed, the resulting four haploid cells are separated from each other by three transverse septa.
A projecting sterigma forms on each pro- mycelium cell, and the haploid nucleus migrates through the sterigma into newly forming basidiospore as it expands at the tip of sterigma.
Mature hyaline and light-sensitive basidiopores are ejected from the sterigmata and carried by air currents to probably limited distances, to infect the alternate host.
Infection results in the production of flask-shaped pycnia, usually in the up- per leaf surface.
The pycnium produces receptive hyphae and small, thin-walled pycniospores which exude from the tip of the pycnium in a drop of pycnial nectar.
The nectar is attractive to insects that, along with rain splashing, brushing of leaves or larger animals, serve to disseminate pycnio- spores among pycnia.
Pycniospores serve as the male gam- etes and consist mainly of a single haploid nucleus with little surrounding cytoplasm.
Flexuos hyphae extend out of the top of the pycnia and serves as the female gametes.
When a pycniospore of one mating type contacts flexu- ous hyphae in a pycnium of the other mating type, fusion 39 Cereal rusts – history, biology and control.
The dikaryotic stage is established with nuclear division and paired association of + and – mating type nuclei.
Chains of single-celled, dikaryotic aeciospores (Fig. 1C) are produced, which can infect gramineous hosts but not the alternate host.
Aeciospores are hydroscopically released from the ae- cium and are airborne to the gramineous host over long distances.
Infection by aeciospores results in the production of a dense mat of hyphae beneath the host epidemis, where sporophores grow and produce masses of single-celled di- karyotic urediniospores (Fig.
Urediniospores are dispersed by wind and can reinfect the cereal host, repeating asexual cycle within each 7 to 14 days, depending on the rust species and environment condi- tions.
Under field conditions where temperatures vary greatly the cycle can be either lengthened or shortened.
Generally, lower temperatures in the field, at least at the F E H I J C A B D G Fig.
On maturing hosts, uredinia eventually cease pro- duction of urediniospores and begin to produce two-celled teliospores (Fig.
At that stage the infection structure is called a telium (Fig. 1G).
Teliospore stalks remain intact and the spores are not dispersed from the telial pustule (Fig.
The alternate host currently provides little direct inocu- lum of cereal rusts, but may be a mechanism for genetic ex- change between races and perhaps populations.
In most areas of the world, the life cycle of cereal rusts consists of continual uredinial generations.
The fungi spread by airborne urediniospores from one gramineous plant to another and from field to field.
Teliospores have a very short dormancy and basidiospore production is rapid and survival short (Wright and Lennard 1978).
Stakman and Piemeisel provided the first understanding that the formae speciales could be subdivided into races.
This set consisted origin- ally of 12 varieties that consistently ensured uniformity of race identity.
Mains and Jackson used the term ‘differential variety’, but apparently they preferred the term ‘differential strain’ because many wheat varieties at that time were not genetically homogene- ous.
Over time with greater emphasis on varietal purity in crops, the term ‘differential variety’ became generally ac- cepted and ‘differential strain’ disappeared from the litera- ture.
In a series of studies during this period he elucidated the genetics of host-parasite relations and formulated the gene-for-gene hypothesis, one of the most important paradigms in plant pathology.
Al- though any number of differentials may be used, standard sets generally include about 8 to 16 differential varieties.
The best sets of differential varieties have differentials with different sin- gle resistance genes backcrossed into a common genetic background.
Near-isogenic differentials eliminate confoun- ding effects of modifier genes acting on resistance in differ- ent host backgrounds.
Monitoring cereal rusts populations provides informa- tion on race prevalence, fluctuations in the racial composi- tion, arising of new virulence combinations (new races) and effectiveness of resistance genes.
The consistent use of a standard set of differentials has shown that intermediate levels of resis- tance exist in host plants as well (Roelfs 1984).
The development of rusts on cereal hosts occurs during the uredial phase of the fungus.
After urediniospore deposition on the host and its germination, a series of essential struc- tures for the establishment of a successful parasitic relation- ship are formed (Leonard and Szabo 2005).
The germinated spore forms a germ tube, which differentiates a structure called the appressorium when it recognizes the stomata.
Therefore after, inside the plant tissues, a subestomatal vesi- cle, the infective hyphae, the haustorium mother cells and the haustorium are formed.
This growth orientation is maintained through the growth of small germ tube ramifications on cell junctions.
During growth of uredi- niospore germ tube, the basipetal-most region of the cyto- plasm forms long, trailing processes that extend back into the emptied portion of the hypha.
The extensive vacuolation that occurs in this region of the hypha is due to a continued development and enlargement of vacuoles that probably requires new membrane synthesis.
This hypothesis partially explains why the germ tube grows in different sizes before differentiating an appressorium (Collins and Read 1997).
The spatial requirements for appressorium in- duction varies greatly among rust species, however, they usually correspond to the dimensions of the host stomata (Staples 2000).
In rust species P. graminis and P. hordei, 91 to 99% of the germ tubes form appressoria when they reach the plant stomata.
Urediniospores with long germ tubes seem to fail in appressorium differentiation (Hu and Rijken- berg 1998).
Very long or very ramified germ tubes seem to dispose less energy to progress with the plant infection (Niks 1990).
Uredioniospore germination and appressorium forma- tion usually occur at night in the presence of a film of water on the foliar surface.
The development of P. graminis is paralyzed after appressorium formation until the next mour- ning, when its growth is reestablished through light stimu- lus.
Light stimulates the photosynthetic process, which re- duces the internal rate of CO2 in stomata, allowing the ap- pressorium to develop.
After fungal penetration into the substomatal chamber, a substomatal vesicle and infective hyphae are formed.
Infective hyphae differentiate in a haustorium mother cell in about 12 h after inoculation.
An infection peg penet- rates the cellular wall, probably through enzymatic dissolu- tion and mechanical pressure.
Inside of the cellular wall, a specialized cell expands in the periplasmatic space, forming a haustorium, about 24 h after inoculation.
During haustorium development, the fungus penetrates the plant cell wall and invaginates the host plasma membrane.
The plant plasma membrane re- mains intact but becomes specialized in the region surroun- ding the haustorium; this region is referred to as the extra- haustorial membrane.
The region between the haustorial cell wall and the extrahaustorial membrane is the extrahaus- torial matrix.
The haustorium formation is now recognized as a key element in maintenance of biotroph organisms, facilitating their interaction with the host cell.
Thus, the haustorium-host cell interface appears to mediate a dynamic interaction involving extensive trafficking of nutrients and signalling molecules.
Effector proteins are secreted by the pathogen and are postulated to enter the host cytoplasm where their role may be to alter host metabolism and de- fence pathways.
After forma- tion of the first haustoria, infective hyphae form other haus- torium mother cells.
The energy to form the first haustoria is provided by reserves from urediniospores.
Subsequent haustorium formation will be limited by nutrient reduction and will depend on the establishment of a compatible para- sitic interaction, without induction of response defenses.
Host colonization can be facilitated by the pathogen’s pro- duction of phytoalexins and compounds similar to plant hormones (Szabo and Bushnell 2001; Panstruga 2003; Leo- nard and Szabo 2005).
Infection process of the cereal rusts is a highly regulated response system that involves signaling and response in both host and pathogen.
In the first stages of intercellular development, the fungus produces a series of metabolic compounds that trigger the resistance mechanisms in sur- rounding cells of host plants.
This change is characterized by massive increases of respi- ration and accumulation of cytokinins in the infected area.
It is the most widespread of the three types of wheat rusts.
The other two are stem rust, caused by Puccinia gra- minis Pers.:Pers.
In the USA, in epidemic years from 1918 to 1976, yield reductions due to wheat stem rust were of 50% or more.
Wheat stripe rust was more restricted in distribution, even though losses up to 70% in commercial fields were recor- ded (Roelfs 1978).
Losses caused by leaf rust can be over 50% in severe epi- demics if fungicides are not used.
Losses estimated at US$ 170 million were caused by epidemics on 10 important cultivars grown in the region during the period 1996-2003.
Stripe rust is more important in the wheat area in southern Chile, where a severe epidemic occurred in 1940.
Incidence of stem rust historically has been more sporadic, but it caused higher levels of damage during severe epidemics.
During 1975-1976 widespread epidemics occurred in Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay, even under unusually favorable environmental conditions.
Severe epidemics of cereal rusts have been recorded in India since the early 1800’s (Joshi 1976).
In Europe, stripe rust and leaf rust are mostly associated with cereal rust losses.
In China, winter wheat production also is affected by recurrent epidemics of stripe rust.
In 2007 and beyond, the world could be facing an even more devastating situation with the outbreak of stem rust race Ug99 in eastern Africa.
Damages could total US$ 1-2 billion in Asia alone, based on a 10% yield loss estimate and depending on market price.
In the end of the crop cycle, when the plant reaches maturity and the environment becomes more unfavorable, the pustules start to produce teliospores in re- placement of the urediniospores.
These spores are two- celled, have thicker walls and darker color (Samborski 1985).
The main source of initial inoculum of P. triticina in each crop season is wheat plants close to the area or volunteers plants, which form the so-called “green bridge”.
The primary alternative host (Thalictrum speciosisimum) does not have an important role in the production of initial 43 Cereal rusts – history, biology and control.
Epidemics of wheat rusts, as well as other diseases, are affected by the three components of the “triangle of the epidemic”: pathogen, host and environment.
The environmental conditions for the survival of P. tri- ticina are the same as those required for the survival of the host leaves.
For instance, at 10°C 12 h of surface wetness is necessary for infection to take place.
The urediniospores germi- nate after 30 min of contact with free water, at temperatures between 15 and 25°C.
At higher and constant temperatures (25°C), sporulation can occur within 7-10 days after uredi- niospore germination and penetration of the fungus, which takes place through the stomata.
At low temperatures (10- 15°C) or with varying diurnal temperatures, longer periods are necessary.
The maximum sporulation occurs about four days after the initial sporulation, at temperatures around 20°C.
The urediniospores can be disseminated by wind over long distances (Hirst and Hurst 1967).
The epidermis is drastically broken by the uredia, giving a rough aspect to the surface of the affected tissue.
The uredia produce urediniospores with brown-red color, and usually are more prolonged and larger than the leaf rust, Fig.
As the wheat matures, the uredospores are replaced by teliospores (Leo- nard and Szabo 2005).
The epidemiology of P. graminis f. sp. tritici is similar to that of P. triticina.
This cha- racteristic makes the stem rust more important at the end of the crop season, for varieties with longer cycles or in late- sowing areas.
Wheat stem rust also differs from leaf rust for requesting a larger wetness period of the tissue (6 to 8 h).
The uredia usually survive for longer periods than leaf rust, however, the rate of development of both diseases is similar.
The main alternative host of P. g. f. sp. tritici is the bush Berberis spp.
Stripe rust Stripe or yellow rust is characterized by uredia distributed in lines or stripes that extend along the leaf between the vascular bundles (Fig. 5).
Besides the non random distribu- tion pattern, the uredia of stripe rust also differ from other wheat rusts for being smaller and for producing yellow- clear urediniospores.
Similar to leaf and stem rusts, in years of severe epidemics strip rust uredia can also affect other green parts of the plant.
As the plants mature the production of urediniospores ceases and is substituted by teliospores (Chen 2005).
Similarly to leaf rust, the urediniospores of stripe rust need a wetness period of 3 h for the germination and infection to take place (Chen 2005).
BARLEY RUSTS Distribution and economic importance Barley (Hordeum vulgare L.) is the world’s fourth most im- portant cereal crop after wheat, maize and rice.
Four rust types occur on barley: leaf rust, caused by Puccinia hordei Otth (syn.
The damage caused on barley depends on the develop- mental stage the plant is at the moment of infection.
The epidemics that happen before or during the flowering period cause the largest reductions in yield.
The rusts increase the respiration and transpiration of the plant, reducing photo- synthesis, vigor and growth of roots, besides the production of withered grains (Mathre 1985).
However, the uredial and telial stages are morphologically distinct from the rust caused by this pathogen on oats, Lolium spp.
The first damages caused by the disease were repor- ted in Nebraska (USA) in 1991.
Currently, it is widespread in many regions of North America, mainly in the mid-west.
Since the first report of the disease in 1991, it has oc- curred every year with different intensities.
Barley stem rust is a disease of sporadic occurrence but in years with favorable weather conditions can cause large yield decreases, as the infected plants produce withered grains.
The intensity of the damage is proportional to the time of occurrence of the disease.
The earlier the disease occurs, the greater the severity will be and consequently damage to the seeds.
Generally when environmental condi- tions are not favorable to disease development, control is relatively ease.
The most common forms are P. graminis f. sp. tritici and P. graminis f. sp. secalis (the rust species at-tacking wheat and rye).
Their occurrence depends on the region, although the formae speciales of wheat seems to be more important on barley.
Barley stripe rust, also known as yellow rust, can cause yield damage of up to 50% and is common under favorable conditions and lack of chemical treatment.
The quality of malt is impaired under conditions of severe infection (Line 2002).
There are no reports of the occurrence of alternate hosts and sexual stage.
The penetration of the stomata occurs via an apres- sorium and penetration peg.
The formation of substomatal vesicles, hyphae and intercellular haustoria, with a knob or globular form, complete the process of infection.
This pro- cess takes around 6-8 h and the production of secondary inoculum from the first infection occurs in about 10 days (Mathre 1985).
In countries where the alternate host is not present their germination, if occurs, is not a source for new infections (Mathre 1985; Hollaway and Horsham 2008a).
The life cycle is complex and involves the alternate host Ornithogalum umbellatum L., known as the Star of Bethle- hem.
Other species of Ornithogalum can also be alternate hosts, allowing the formation of picnia and aecia.
The main sources of initial inoculum in regions of bar- ley production are urediniospores.
These are spread to long distances and can remain from one season to another on voluntary plants.
The disease develops quickly at tempera- tures between 15 and 22°C, when the humidity is not a limiting factor.
The system of production affects the occurrence, deve- lopment and percentage of damage caused by leaf rust on barley.
The fertilization with nitrogen can increase the oc- currence of rust as the absence of rains at the end of the crop can reduce its occurrence.
Low altitude (<2500 m) may increase the disease intensity, while altitudes over 2500 m are associated with its reduction.
Crown rust Crown rust are characterized by orange linear pustules, usu- ally associated with chlorosis, occurring mostly on the blade of leaves and occasionally on sheaths, stems and owns.
The name “crown rust” is due to the appearance of teliospores, which have appendices on the apex conferring a crown aspect.
The remaining teliospores on barley debris and other susceptible cereals germinate and produce basidio- spores that infect the alternate host, Rhamnus cathartica, where pycnial and aecial stages occur.
The aeciospores pro- duced on R. cathartica are the primary source of inoculum for barley and the infection can occur before the extrusion of the third leaf.
Crown rust develops at temperatures around 20 to 25°C during the daytime and between 15 to 20°C at night, associated with high humidity.
The urediniospores need a film of free water on the surface of the leaves to germinate.
Penetration occurs via stomata, through apressoria at tem- peratures between 10 and 25°C and the infection is inhib- ited at temperatures above 30°C (USDA-ARS 2008).
Also, it infects some species of Brachypodium, Bromus, Festuca, and Lolium, from the tribe Poeae, and Phalaris from the tribe Avenae.
All these species are epidemiologically im- portant because they contribute to increase the inoculum of P. coronata (Jin and Steffenson 1999, 2002; USDA-ARS 2008).
At the end of the season pustules produce teliospores of dark color, which remain on the dead tissues.
The alternate hosts, where the aecial and pycnial stages occur, are species of Berberis (B. vulgaris, B. canadensis Mill. and B. fend- leri) and some species of Mahonia.
Conditions of high tem- peratures and humidity favor the occurrence of the disease.
The optimum temperature for development is 20°C, tempe- ratures below 15 and above 40°C are limiting to the occur- rence of the disease.
Thus, the disease is of greater econo- mic importance in areas where such conditions are present throughout the crop season (Mathre 1985; Hollaway and Horsham 2008a, 2008b).
Stripe rust Symptoms of stripe rust usually occur earlier than leaf and stem rust in the crop season.
The pustules are yellow and occur mainly on leaves and spikes, often linearly and parallel to the vascular bundles, except at the seedling stage, where the pustules occur randomly.
The pustules quickly cover the leaves and often the spike, leading the plant to become dry.
The germ tubes can penetrate directly into the stomata, without needing to form apressoria and a penet- ration peg.
At the end of the season dark teliospores, pos- sessing a short period of dormancy, are produced.
The inoculum can be successfully dissemi- nated by more than 800 km from the point of origin (Za- doks 1965).
The development of the disease is faster between 10 and 15°C with moisture available.
In the presence of dew and temperatures between 2 and 15°C ger- mination and formation of apressorium occur.
The latent period of pustules is also dependent on temperature, where tem- peratures between 0 and 10°C inhibit it but do not stop the development of the fungus.
It is the third most important winter crop in southern Brazil (Leonard and Martinelli 2005).
Both attack all species of oats, including wild oats (Wall- work 1992) and are well recognized diseases, occurring almost everywhere these crops are grown (Zillinsky 1983).
Crown rust is the most harmful oat disease and is dis- tributed worldwide.
As a consequence of the induced physiological stress, grain yields are negatively correlated with crown rust severity.
The damage is more pronounced at the earliest stages of crop development.
The economic threshold of the disease is very low, around 15-20% of foliar incidence or 0.2 to 0.3% of plant severity.
These losses are consequence of the aggressive- ness of the pathogen population, the lack of effective resis- tance genes and the favorable environmental conditions for long periods.
After some weeks, the bor- ders of the uredia can turn black, with the formation of teliospores.
The urediniospores and aeciospores of P. c. f. sp. avenae are spread widely by wind and can reach long distances.
Their germination needs free water on the leaf surface and the infection occurs through the stomata.
Prevailing wind patterns annually distribute uredinio- spores of P. coronata in a cyclical pattern throughout the oat-growing regions of Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay as a shared epidemiological system.
Epidemics typically start early; sometimes while Avena spp. is still at the tillering stage of development.
Avena strigosa is less susceptible than A. sativa, but rust severities of 5-10% are common during the crop season (Leonard and Martinelli 2005).
These in- fections produce aecidia from which aeciospores arise and then infect the oats.
Stem rust Oat stem rust symptoms most commonly appear on the stems and leaf sheaths, but leaf blades and spikes may also become infected.
Urediniospores develop in pustules (ure- dia) that rupture the epidermis and expose masses of red- dish brown spores (Fig.
The pustules are larger than those of crown rust, oval shaped or elongated, with loose or torn epidermal tissue along the margins.
After that, teliospores develop, either in the same uredia or in different fruiting structures called telia (Martinelli 2004).
Epidemics are more probable to occur when tempe- ratures are warm (15-30°C) and conditions moist (Wallwork 1992).
RYE RUSTS Rye (Secale cereale L.) is second only to wheat among the grains most commonly used in the production of bread.
In Argentina, it is an im- portant pasture crop, and in southern Australia, it is planted to prevent wind erosion.
Rye is also a particularly important crop in Poland, Germany, and three republics of the former Soviet Union.
Rye can be infected by three different types of rusts: leaf rust, caused by P. recon- dita f. sp. secalis Roberge, crown rust, caused by P. coro- nata var.
Leaf rust Rye leaf rust is widely distributed in the regions where rye is grown.
The pustules are small, circular, and orange- colored, and are distributed on the leaves and sheaths.
As the plants mature, the pustules become dark in color due to the development of telia.
Yield losses can reach up to 40% under natural conditions of in- fection.
The most marked characteristics are the teliospores with elongated and branched appendages, in addition to the broad pathogenicity to the tribe Triticeae.
The pustules of crown rust on rye are similar to those found in barley.
They occur mainly in the leaf blades and can appear on sheaths, stems and owns.
The alternate host is Rhamnus cathartica (Jin and Steffenson 1999; USDA-ARS 2008).
It is considered the most important disease of the crop in Brazil.
With the progress of the disease, pus- tules appear brown with a format that varies from oval to elongated, alone or in clusters, on stem, leaf sheaths and leaves.
Understanding the epidemiology of a disease is essential before starting any control strategy, especially one invol- Fig.
The most effective means of controlling the cereal rusts is the combination of cultural control practices with disease resistance and per- haps fungicide applications.
No single practice is effective under all conditions, but using a series of cultural practices greatly enhances the existing resistances.
However, care must be taken not to permit uredi- niospores of the cereal rusts to escape outside their epide- miological areas.
Since then, host re- sistance (Fig. 9) has become one of the primary control me- thods of plant diseases and a priority objective of plant breeding (Byerlee 1996).
The likelihood of resistance breakdown increases considerably if these race-specific resistance genes are the only source of resistance in cultivars releases to farmers.
Race-specific resistance genes typically break- down within 5 years of deployment (Singh and Huerta- Spino 2001).
Genetic resistance to wheat rusts Among the breeding programs for rust resistance, some have been successful for a number of years.
The greatest successes have been against stem rust, perhaps because of the nature of the pathogen and perhaps due to the greater number of scientific years of study and work.
In Australia, a series of cultivars with Sr26 have been released since 1971 and have grown on nearly 1 million ha without stem rust losses (Luig and Rajaram 1972).
The adult plant resistance gene Sr2 derived from Hope results in an absence of uredinia in the internode tissues (Hare and McIntosh 1979; Sunder- wirth and Roelfs 1980).
This has been probably the most commonly used Sr resistance gene worldwide since the 1940s.
The genes for wheat leaf rust resistance have been obtained primarily from cultivars of T. aestivum, but some are from other Triticum spp.
Gene Lr34 together with other un-named slow rus- ting genes is believed to be involved in the durable resis- tance of ‘Frontana’ and other wheats (Singh and Rajaram 1992).
Seventy genes with official (Yr followed by a number) or provisional (Yr fol- lowed by letters) symbols have been reported (Chen 2005).
Some CIMMYT germplasm-de- rived cultivars, such as ‘Anza’ (Yr18) and ‘Pavon 76’, also have durable resistance (Singh and Rajaram 1994).
At least 26 different resistance genes were described for barley stripe rust in 18 barley lines (Chen and Line 2003).
However, the genetic base for rust resistance is very narrow and there is no single gene effective to all races.
Amongst the crown rust resistance genes known, 97 are race-specific, named Pc genes (Pc1 to Pc96 and PcX).
Plants with genotypes Pc frequently respond to P. coronata through the development of a hypersensiti- vity reaction (HR), with death of cells at the local infection site.
Two loci seem to control cellular death: Rds suppress the HR reaction, but not resistance, mediated by the resis- tance gene Pc82.
In contrast, locus Rih confers HR to resis- tant as well as to susceptible plants.
Data showed that the locus Rds is not linked to the cluster Pca, while the Rih locus is intimately linked to it.
This indicates that many variables affect the development of HR suggesting that HR may not be essential to crown rust resistance.
Despite the vast number of known race-specific genes, only a few of them have good potential to be used in breeding programs.
Regarding oat stem rust, there is a much more limited reservoir of resistance against, but known genes can provide effective and long term resistance when used in appropriate combinations.
Genetic resistance to rye rusts Compared with other cereals such as wheat and barley, little information is available about the inheritance of resistance to rye leaf rust.
Resistance genes conferring specific resis- tance are more studied, although slow rusting resistance has also been reported.
The rye resistance gene SrR seems to be a promising source of resistance to stem rust, and, just like gene Sr31, will be able to be transferred to wheat.
When genetic resistance is overcome or when its level is in- sufficient to control cereal rusts, chemical control is needed.
Chemical control has been successfully used in Europe, per- mitting high yields (6 to 7 t/ha) and where prices for wheat are warranted (Stubbs and de Bruin 1970; Buchenauer 1982).
Fungicide use prevented multimillion dollar losses, and in recent years, use of fungi- cides has successfully reduced yield damage caused by stripe rust.
Nevertheless, the use of fungicides adds a huge cost to wheat production, which is a burden for many growers, especially in developing countries.
The use of fungi- cides to control wheat rusts differs among countries.
Fungi- cides have been recommended since 1977 in Brazil, have been used widely in Paraguay since 1976, and have been more commonly used in Uruguay since the 1990s.
In nor- mal epidemic conditions at least 2 applications of fungicides are required to control the disease on highly susceptible cul- tivars.
In Argentina, one fungicide application to control leaf rust is used on about 35% of the wheat area.
Cultural practices Some cultural practices can also help, at least partially, in the control of cereal rusts.
The “green-bridge” formed by volunteer cereals plants guarantees the mainte- nance and dissemination of inoculum between crop seasons or between areas with different sowing dates.
Removing this “green-bridge” with tillage of herbicides is an effective control measure for rust epidemics that would result from endogenous inoculum.
The vulnerability of commercial cul- tivars to rust epidemics can be reduced through broadening the genetic basis in breeding programs.
In some areas, control of timing, frequency and amount of irrigation and fertilization applications can aid in disease control.
On large farms, it may help if fields are arranged so that the early maturing cultivars are downwind from late maturing cultivars.
Eradication efforts by individual growers probably would not result in visible gains im- mediately in stem rust control due to large amounts of ase- xual inoculum.
The alternate host for leaf rust may function more as a source of sexual reproduction than a source of epidemic-generating inoculum.
Rhamnus is difficult to control and ex- tensive infestations still remain particularly in Ontario, Ca- nada (Harder and Haber 1992).
The cereal rusts are the most striking and fascinating of the plant pathogens.
Obviously, the devastating and even catas- trophic effect of rust epidemics on cereal host populations was, since early records, the first factor of notoriety for these pathogens.
However, cereal rusts once again showed that their millenary coevolution with cereals had taught them to survive.
The cycles of boom-and-bust, where resistant cultivars were released and quickly overcame by rust pathogens were another striking feature of the cereal rusts.
Fortunately, durable forms of resistance to cereals rusts were detected and their genetic control has been compre- hensively studied.
Differences in resis- tance levels appear to be related to signaling and to the in- tensity at which these mechanisms are expressed.
Thus, efficient genetic markers associated with the genes involved in the defense process can be obtained.
Genomic studies of the fungi-causing cereal rusts and the discovery of mechanisms involved in non-host interactions, such as rice and cereal rusts, are also great challenges for the future.

Although resistant varieties have been developed, the fungus tends to overcome new sources resistance very quickly.
Plants have evolved a single gene (R genes) defense network that can recognize specific pathogen effectors (Avr), in a gene-for-gene manor.
In rusts, effectors are secreted proteins responsible for inducing the uptake of nutrients and inhibit host defense responses.
Identification of secreted proteins during the infection may help to understand the mode of infection of P. triticina.
Little is known about molecular interactions in the pathosystem wheat-leaf rust and no Avr genes from cereal rusts have been cloned.
From 432 EST’s derived from haustoria and infected plants, fifteen secreted proteins were identified and 10 were selected as potential avirulence candidates.
Pt3 and Pt 51 are two P. triticina (Pt) candidates expressed specifically in the haustoria and encode small cysteine-rich secreted proteins.
Eight candidates are expressed at early stages of infection, during spore germination and 6 days after inoculation.
They also do not share a conserved motif with known filamentous fungus Avr proteins.
Pt3, Pt12 and Pt27 were tested by transient expression experiments using co-bombardment with GUS into leaf rust resistant isogenic lines.
Reduction in the expression of reporter gene GUS co-expressed with Pt27 indicates a potential avirulence factor for Lr26 in wheat.
